7. RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
7.1 The Committee was informed that the Department supports nearly 1200 research projects each year
in Basic, Discovery and Translational Research in the areas of Agriculture and allied areas including
Animal Biotechnology and Aquaculture, Healthcare including Vaccine, Drugs, Medical Devices and Implants,
Bio-engineering, Food and Nutrition, Environment and Clean Energy and Industrial Biotechnology. The
Committee notes that during the period (2015-2017), 5724 proposals were received, out of which
only 542 (9.46%) proposals/projects have been funded so far.

8
8. BASIC RESEARCH
8.1 The Secretary of the Department informed the Committee that through Basic Research in Modern
Biology has been funding basic research in a wide variety of biological science field with a goal of
exploiting new knowledge to enhance and where possible transform-future capabilities. Noteworthy
achievements of some of the projects supported are: Functional characterization of sugar- and auxin-
regulated DUF581 domain containing genes encoding expressed proteins of unknown functions in model
plant system has led to the identification of a novel class of plant-specific zinc finger proteins, studies
on chromatin remodeling for activation of systemic acquired resistance in Arabidopsis has revealed an
epigenetic regulator that modulates both flowering and SAR, research work being carried out by scientists
at Delhi University and IIT Delhi on development of potent small molecule inhibitors against dopamine
beta-hydroxylase to combat cardiovascular diseases has led to the discovery of five small molecules as
potent anti-hypertensive etc.
8.2 The Committee is of the view that making potable water available to our citizens is one of
the biggest challenges facing our country. The Committee feels that the Department of
Biotechnology has the potential to devise a technology to convert the filthiest of the water into
potable water. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should include
developing technologies for extracting safe drinking water from available water resources to
lessen the problem of drinking water in the country.
9. AGRICULTURE AND ALLIED AREAS: CROP BIOTECHNOLOGY
9.1 Further the Committee was informed that Agriculture biotechnology programme deals with a wide
range of economically important crops including rice, wheat, cotton, millets, oilseeds and pulses. DBT
supported these projects for managing various biotic and abiotic stresses and improving yield and quality
traits of the existing crops which has been a priority for the country. These research projects are
supported and implemented in networks, centre of excellence as well as individual investigator driven
projects. During the period, a total of 65 research publications and 4 patent applications were generated
and 31 M.Sc. and 37 PhD students completed their degrees involved in R&D projects of agriculture
biotechnology programme. Key focus of the programme is on product oriented basic research, product
development translational research and bio-safety research using technologies like Genetic Engineering,
Marker Assisted Breeding, Genome based breeding, Genome editing etc. Area aims at enhancement of
crop productivity and nutrition, pest and disease protection, and abiotic stresses with focus on drought
and flooding. The major achievements of the programme include:
• New genes potentially involved in root development, abiotic stress response, nutrient acquisition,
phosphate utilization and nodulation have been identified in rice and chickpea and their modes
of action were demonstrated in model plant.
• Proof of concept of transgenic rice lines and advanced generation transgenic chickpea lines
with high root growth have been developed.
• Rust and Late Leaf Spot, resistant backcross lines of groundnut developed which gave ~15%
higher yield than the recurrent parent.

9
• Twenty soybean homozygous lines with Phytophthora and powdery mildew resistance were
developed through molecular markers.
• Molecular characterization of calcium signaling and transport machinery of finger millet
(Eleusinecoracana) was undertaken for calcium biofortification and Finger millet germplasm
with high calcium content (452.8mg/100gm) has been characterized and registered.
• Biotic stress resistant rice varieties have been developed through marker assisted breeding.
9.2 The Committee appreciates the achievement realised by the Department in the field of crop
biotechnology. The Committee is of the view that agriculture, alongwith its allied sectors, is the
largest livelihood activity in our country and it is the need of the hour that we all should work
in tandem to improve our crops productivity with the help of technological advancements and
sustainable technologies by establishing a dissemination network so that the innovations reach
the last point.
9.3 The Committee also feels that out of box thinking is required to tap the potential lying in
our agricultural activities. The Committee recommends the Department to take necessary steps
in the direction of untapped potential with the help of its biotechnological strategic interventions
so as to address the issues of not only the crops productivity but also for mitigation of post
harvest loss and enhancing the nutritional value as well.
10. ANIMAL BIOTECHNOLOGY
10.1 The Committee was informed that livestock production is becoming increasingly important to
economic growth of the country and therefore application of biotechnological tools to enhance the
productivity of livestock sector is continued through R&D interventions supported by the Department.
Major achievements include: the structural and functional characterization of follicle stimulation hormone
(FSH) of marmoset, transcript of buffalo pregnancy associated glycoproteins (PAgs) were identified,
amplified, cloned, sequenced and compared with the existing database to confirm the predominant
transcript in buffalo placentome, the urinary proteins SLAMF9 (Signaling lymphocyte activation molecule
family-9), MARK1 (Microtubule Affinity-Regulating Kinase 1) and PDK1 (Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Kinase,
Isozyme 1) were identified as possible marker having biological significance during pregnancy etc.
11. ANIMAL HEALTH
11.1 The Department shared with the Committee that it is supporting R&D programmes for development
of affordable new generation vaccines and diagnostics against various animal diseases of economic
importance. The emphasis is given to the 'commercialization of the leads, products and processes
developed in the R & D programmes. During the period (2015-17), several new projects have been
supported on epidemiological studies of mastitis, development of therapeutics for brucellosis, development
of diagnostics for theileriosis, and development of vaccines against Hemorrhagic septicaemia, Infectious
Bursal disease, Porcine circovirus, Hepatitis Hydropericardium Syndrome virus, etc. The Network Program
on Brucellosis has successfully completed the first phase. A repository was established for storing and
cataloguing different Brucella species. A novel penside diagnostic, lateral flow assay kit, indirect ELISA
kit against Brucella species and a hand held ELISA reader have been developed. Other major achievements

10
include more that 50 research publications, 10 patent applications filed, 08 technologies developed and
04 commercialized.
11.2 The Committee notes the activities undertaken by the Department in the field of animal
biotechnology and animal health. The Committee, nonetheless, is of the opinion that the rate of
commercialisation of the technologies developed by the Department is not very encouraging and
it reflects that the technologies so developed by the Department either are not as per the
requirements of the industry or there may be flaws in the technologies restricting their
commercialisation. Hence, the Committee desires the Department to take market driven research
activities so that the technologies developed by it are well received by the industry.
11.3 The Committee also feels that the Department needs to augment its research activities in
the direction of disease resistance in our indigenous livestock. The Committee, therefore,
recommends the Department to take necessary action in these directions.
11.4 The Committee is further of the view that the Department should also adopt more focused
approach towards increasing the productivity of the indigenous varieties of cows in the country;
establishment of sperm banks so as to make available hybrid indigenous sperm of high quality
and standards; etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take
necessary action in this regard.
12. AQUACULTURE AND MARINE BIOTECHNOLOGY
12.1 The Committee was informed that aquaculture plays a very important role in Indian agricultural
economy. The programme is being implemented for enhancing aquaculture production and productivity
and development of useful product and processes from marine resources. During the period (2015-2017)
several projects have been supported to benefit the aquatic and marine sectors by addressing broad areas
on fish genomics, proteomics and transcriptomics, antimicrobial and immunostimulant, fish health and
nutrition, development of bioactive molecules and biomaterials, bio-surfactants, biomarker, marine
actinobacteria, DNA bar coding of marine ascidians and development of diagnostics and vaccines through
adoption of molecular tools and techniques. Some of the major achievements of the programme are: (i)
development of an ELISA-based kit for detection of IgM of Indian major carps against Aeromonas
hydrophila infection (ii) a Lateral Flow Immuno Assay has been developed for toxinotyping (iii) a nano
delivery system of DNA based RNAi vaccine against WSSV in tiger shrimp has been developed (iv) RT-
PCR based detection of viable Salmonella and Vibrio cholera from fresh and processed finfish and
shellfish has been developed. (iv) anti-WSSV formulation was made as a prophylactic measure in shrimp
health management (vi) 50 Cell lines have been developed from 24 fish species. 14 patents have been
filed for product/ process development and 07 technologies have been successfully transferred to Industry
for commercialization.
12.2 The Committee notes that India has a coastline of over 8000 kms. and ranks 2nd in global
fish production, inland capture and aquaculture. The Committee, however, feels that sustainable
productivity and management has been a concern area where the Department of Biotechnology
needs to take the required strategic policy interventions. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Department should take necessary biotechnological measures to address the issues of
sustainable productivity and management.

11
12.3 The Committee is also of the opinion that health of the aquatic animal predominantly
depends on the health of the aquaculture ecosystem. Thus, development of healthy brood stock
of all cultivable fin and shell fishes assumes greater importance and the Committee feels that
the Department of Biotechnology can play a crucial role on this count. The Committee, therefore,
recommends the Department to take necessary strategic measures to develop high health brood
stock.
12.4 The Committee is of the opinion that the biological diversity of the marine resources along
the Indian coast in the form of creeks, estuaries, deep seas and continental shelf offer enormous
scope for the discovery of novel products and processes which have application in biomass and
food production, production of polymers, biocatalysts, biomedical products, and organics;
bioremediation and biomining etc. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Department
should work out a roadmap for the purpose and put earnest efforts in this direction. The
Committee is hopeful that with the help of right policy interventions, the Department can write
a new chapter of biotechnological advancements in the field of aquaculture and marine bio-
technology.
13. MEDICINAL AND AROMATIC PLANTS
13.1 Programme has been remodelled in the last year focusing on taking forward the research leads to
their logical conclusion through multi-disciplinary approach. An end-to-end demonstration project on field
evaluation of Cymbopogon flexuosus (lemongrass), Cymbopogon winterianus (citronella) and Cymbopogon
martinii (palmarosa) covering an area of 53.5 acre in the farmers' fields involving 10 villages of Dhar
block (Kandi area) in Punjab completed. Three farm distillation units were installed and made operational
in adopted village clusters. The marketing of essential oil has been provided through linkage organizations.
The capacity building of farmers was carried out on cultivation, harvesting and processing operations
through 59 on-farm contact programmes, 25 awareness programmes and six exposure visits. A technology
transfer agreement has been signed between ICGEB, New Delhi and Sun Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd.,
Gurugram for clinical development of most bioactive fraction (CiPa) from Cissampelos pareira towards
developing a phytopharmaceutical drug for dengue infection.
13.2 The Committee takes note of the various activities undertaken under Medicinal and Aromatic
Plants. The Committee observes that the Department has been supporting the salient aspects of
the Indian medicine system through its research activities. The Committee, however, feels that
the Department has to keep pace with the increasing attention about the medicinal and aromatic
plants among the urban population and take necessary measures to tap the unlimited potential
of these plants with the help of its biotechnological capabilities.
14. MISSION INNOV ATION - ACCELERATING THE CLEAN ENERGY
Revolution
14.1 The 'Mission Innovation' was launched during PM's visit to Paris in November 2015. Besides India
and US, 23 other countries are members of this initiative led by US to drive forward clean energy
innovation in a global scale. Under the initiative, members have pledged to double their collective investments
in energy R&D funding of over USD 15 Billion annually to over 30 billion by 2021. DBT has been

12
identified as nodal agency to coordinate national efforts in clean energy for Mission Innovation activities
on behalf of Government of India. Department of Science & Technology, Ministry of Power, Ministry
of New and Renewable Energy are other Ministries participating in addressing the challenges. India will
be partnering in all the challenges. India will be leading the Smart Grids innovation challenge and co-lead
the sustainable biofuels innovation challenge and is collaborating in all the challenges identified. 7 innovation
challenges has been launched, these challenges are global calls to action that complement efforts already
underway by Mission Innovation countries.
14.2 The Committee notes the work done so far by the Department in the direction of biofuels.
However, lot more is yet to be achieved on this count. The Committee hopes that the Department,
along with other related agencies of the Government, will continue its concerted efforts and will
work in tandem to realise the targets set for biofuels.
14.3 The Committee is of the view that the Department should also chalk out a policy initiative
and set up Bioenergy based incubation centres across the country so as to provide a platform to
have interface between academia and industry. If required, the Department should seek budgetary
support for the purpose at RE stage. The Committee also recommends that the Department
should focus on nurturing start-ups in this direction.
15. NANOBIOTECHNOLOGY
15.1 The recent focus of the Nanobiotechnology programme has been on implementation and monitoring
of translational research projects to develop products in various areas such as nanomedicine for cancer,
kalazar, smart Nano-carries to deliver drug in brain, imaging and contrast agents, diagnostics for detection
of pathogens and disease biomarkers, Nanosensor to detect metabolic diseases related biomarkers,
development of Nano patch for wound healing, and continue to support such proposals with translational
values. Activities are initiated to set up infrastructure/system to promote translational research and
product development. An ideation system has been created to enhance the innovative potential of the
proposals through setting up dynamic and interactive website/supporting programs for idea generation.
The total number of patents filed during the period 2016-17 is 05 and 57 research publications.
15.2 The Committee is of the view that the application of nanotechnology can play a very
important and crucial role in the areas of agriculture, health, food, environment, etc. The
Committee feels that the Department should continue its activities in this direction and also
explore the possibilities to address the challenges posed to our agriculture, health, food and
environment with the help of advancement in the field of the nanotechnology.
16. MEDICAL BIOTECHNOLOGY AND RELATED AREAS:
INFECTIOUS DISEASES
16.1 The mandate of the program is to establish an integrated R&D approach for the development of
preventive, therapeutic and diagnostic tools for infectious diseases. Research & Development activities
in the important infectious diseases caused by various pathogenic agents including bacteria, viruses,
parasites, fungi etc. viz., HIV/AIDS, Hepatitis, Influenza, Chikungunya, Dengue, Malaria, Leishmaniasis,
etc. have been funded. Major achievements include: (i) the study on the effects of interaction of Hepatitis
C Virus protein NS5A with host translation machinery on HCV pathogenesis has revealed that HCV NS5A

13
sequesters eukaryotic cap binding protein eIF4E to 40S ribosome and forms a complex ENR (ii) over
the years many compounds of medicinal value have been isolated from Indian Medicinal Plants. Recently
a search found potent anti HCV activity to be present in the semi-purified sub-fraction of methanolic
extract prepared from V . wallichii root (iii) the human hepatic endothelial cell SK Hep1 was adapted to
growth in 3D under hydrogel conditions and maximum growth inhibitory effect of DV2 & 3 NS1 was
seen by direct exogenous exposure (iv) a study on assured-chip, an accurate, affordable and rapid
microfluidics-based diagnosis of Hepatitis-C virus has demonstrated a fully integrated isothermal PCR
assay onto a POC (point-of-care) device for rapid and on-site molecular diagnosis of Hepatitis-C virus
(v) studies in Phase I of the project established that curcumin- arteether combination therapy is very
effective in the treatment of parasite (P. berghei) recrudescence and cerebral malaria in mice and the
studies have been extended to nanocurcumin (PLGA-curcumin) to examine whether it is superior to
native curcumin in view of the poor bioavailability of native curcumin.
16.2 DBT-ICMR Collaborative Efforts on HIV/AIDS and Microbicides have been launched. A new multi
country collaborative initiative, co-ordinated by Canadian institute of Health Research and WHO, to
establish a Healthy Life Trajectories initiative (HeLTi) based on developmental origin of health and
diseases.
16.3 The Committee is of the opinion that a diagnostic test kit for TB patients is the need of the
hour so as to enable early detection of TB. The Committee also feels that the Department should
in coordination with Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and ICMR devise innovative
technologies for the purpose.
16.4 The Committee is also of the view that the Department should undertake an awareness
campaign to popularise its technological advancements and sensitise all the State Governments
as well as medical colleges about the diagnosis and clinical symptomatic diagnosis of TB so as to
provide an important breakthrough in the early detection of the disease.
16.5 The Committee expresses concerns on the issue of mosquito breeding which appears to have
gone out of control. The Committee is of the view that the Department of Biotechnology should
play a significant role by devising technology to keep the mosquito population under control and
should examine the genda flower like pyrethrum for the purpose. Similarly, the Department
should take research work on pheromone traps for the female mosquito.
17. BIODESIGN PROGRAMME
17.1 Biodesign program has been implemented as a flagship program of the Department for fostering and
promoting development of indigenous affordable medical technologies and creating an ecosystem for
med-tech innovations and entrepreneurship in the country. The major achievement during the period
(i) development of diagnostic tests for MTb, acute febrile syndrome (ii) development of platform
technologies for improved stability and yield of recombinant protein (iii) design, prototyping and initial
testing of a bed-to-bed patient transfer device (iv) two entrepreneurial ventures are undertaken, two
technologies have been licensed and two technologies commercialized.
17.2 The Committee notes the scientific improvements brought with the support of its research
activities in the field of medical biotechnology and related areas. The Committee hopes that the

14
Department would continue its focus on this sector and further strengthen its activities in the
areas of human genome research, vaccines, infectious, chronic disease biology, stem cells &
regenerative medicine and the biodesign programmes.
18. FOOD AND NUTRITION
18.1 Research and Development endeavors were continued in food biotechnology and nutrition biology,
addressal of micro & macro nutrient deficiencies through development of fortified foods with generation
of clinical evidence and development of novel food products and processes. Projects were funded in two
new areas: (i) Food to Food Fortification and (ii) Addressal of Food Allergy. A programme for "Strengthening
research in the area of Food sciences through an integrated M.Sc - Ph.D programme" in Guwahati
University was initiated in the current year. Other major achievements include: (i) development of the
process technology & machinery for the production of iron fortified rice premix from the broken rice
and an iron fortificant. A pilot scale demonstration facility with a production capacity of 100 kg/day iron
fortified rice premix has been established at IIT Kharagpur. (ii) A state of art whole body potassium
counter to accurately estimate the body cell mass (lean body mass) has been built. (iii) five types of hypo
immunogenic products, namely hypo immunogenic muffins, hypo immunogenic bread, hypo immunogenic
biscuits, hypo immunogenic chapatti and hypo immunogenic spinach pasta were developed.
18.2 The Committee discussed various issues on the subject 'Public Health, Food and Nutrition Biology'
and enquired about the steps taken by the Department to address the issues of Severe Acute Malnutrition
(excessive thinness). Responding to the query, the Secretary, Department of Biotechnology submitted
before the Committee that Severe Acute Malnutrition is listed as a priority condition for reducing
childhood mortality through product based nutrition intervention (Ready to Use Therapeutic Food or
RUTF). It was informed that in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and Indian
Council of Medical Research, the Department has led a National Alliance on SAM to generate scientific
evidence to inform public health policy. The Secretary apprised the Committee that 5 indigenous Therapeutic
Food Formulations in Ready-to-Eat form were developed as per WHO/UNICEF standards for "medical
nutrition therapy" for rehabilitation of severe acute malnourished child. A pilot scale demonstration unit
with 100 kg/day capacity, was designed and developed according to GMP and GLP norms by IIT
Kharagpur. The developed Therapeutic Food Formulations in Ready-to-Eat form and their process
technology was formally transferred to an industry for commercialization. The Secretary also apprised
the Committee that BIBCOL (Bharat Immunologicals and Biologicals) through Department of Biotechnology's
programme support has developed a formulation consisting of a mix of seven minerals & thirteen
vitamins in a sachet aimed for treatment of severely malnourished children. It was brought to the
knowledge of the Committee that BIBCOL is seeking approval from FSSAI for this product.
18.3 The Committee takes note of the activities of the Department in the direction of Food and
Nutrition. The Committee, however, is of the view that the Department should further intensify
its activities to address the issue of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) so as to tackle the stunting
in the children of our country which can lead to developmental problems. The Committee would
also like to be apprised of the status of the approval of FSSAI to the formulation consisting of
a mix of seven minerals and thirteen vitamins in a sachet aimed for treatment of severely
malnourished children.

18.4 The Committee also recommends that the Department should publicise its demonstration
unit developed by IIT, Kharagpur to the various states of the country and sentise and encourage
them to make use of the technology in their respective states to combat Severe Acute Malnutrition
(SAM).
18.5 The Committee is also of the view that the Department should in co-ordination with the
FSSAI take necessary action in the direction of making oil fortification mandatory so as to retain
its nutritional value.
19. BIOTECHNOLOGY FOR SOCIETAL DEVELOPMENT
19.1 Department has been supporting projects aiming to promote use of biotechnological processes and
tools for the benefit of the disadvantaged section of the society comprising women, rural population and
SC/STs in ecologically compatible manner. The programme aims to create platform for self-employment
generation among the target population by diffusion of proven and field-tested technologies through
demonstration, training and extension activities. The projects are being supported in agriculture and
animal husbandry including fish farming, poultry farming, pig production, goat farming, value added
products, floriculture, hybrid seed production, integrated farming system, entrepreneurship development,
bio-resource utilization, women and child health, hygiene and nutrition. Large number of rural, SC/ST
and women population including youth have been benefited through implementation of these projects. A
programme for the rehabilitation of Flash Flood affected area in Uttarakhand is being continued to extend
the benefit to flood affected people of Uttarakhand. A large number of rural farmers including youth, SC/
STs population and women have been benefited through implementation of biotechnology based projects.
19.2 The Committee is of the considered opinion that with the help of right technological
interventions, we can bring the marginalised sections of our society into the mainstream and
make them more productive for the overall growth of the country. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department should further intensify its activities in the directions of
societal development and take necessary steps for creating platform for self-employment generation
in the industrially backward areas of the country.
19.3 The Committee is of the view that the Department of Biotechnology can play a very important
role to address the issue of clean drinking water with the help of its technological advancements.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should chalk out a roadmap for the
purpose and further strengthen its activities in this direction.

21. HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
21.1 The Department is implementing an Integrated Human Resource Development (HRD) Programme
in Biotechnology to cater the needs of the R & D, manufacturing, quality control sector in institutional
and industrial environment. The HRD programme is comprising of post graduate teaching programme,
short term training courses for upgradation of skills of mid-career scientists and faculty engaged in
teaching and R&D, industrial training of students, fellowships for doctoral and post-doctoral research
training in frontier areas of life sciences. India can take pride in being one of the first few countries in
the world to start PG courses in biotechnology.
PG Programs: Two new PG programs viz., M. Tech. Pharma Biotechnology at Institute of
Chemical Technology, Mumbai and M. Tech. Computational Biology at Indraprastha Institute of
Information Technology, New Delhi have been supported.

19
PG Teaching Program: Department is working towards for revision and reframing of model
course curriculum of Post-graduate teaching programmes in Biotechnology. A web based dynamic
portal PROMPT (Review of Mechanism & Protocols of Teaching) has been developed for effectively
capturing feedback of postgraduate students admitted under DBT supported teaching programmes
in universities about quality of teaching programme.
Star College: Star College Scheme is a unique scheme initiated by the Department with an aim
to nurture excellence in science education at Under Graduate level. The main objective was to
strengthen the under-graduate science departments by providing academic and physical infrastructure
to the colleges, imparting hands-on training to UG students, promoting faculty improvement
programme, networking with neighboring colleges and institutions, providing better library facilities,
motivating students towards research and even encouraging out-reach activities for students in the
neighboring school & colleges. There are currently 85 ongoing Colleges. The Star college scheme
was chosen to be the first starting place to explore a pilot programme to bring Foldscope to the
scientific community.
DBT-JRF: The DBT-JRF programme is being supported by Department of Biotechnology since
2004 with an objective to provide opportunities for pursuing Ph.D. in biotechnology. The DBT-
JRF Program has provision to select JRFs according to merit in Biotechnology Entrance Test
(BET) under two Categories namely Category I and Category II. During 2016-17, 6825 applications
were received, 5865 students appeared for the online exam. Merit list of 300 students in category
-I and 112 students in Category-II was announced.
DBT-RA: Department initiated DBT Research Associateship programme in 2001 for providing
post-doctoral exposure in frontier areas of research in Biotechnology in premier institutes engaged
in major biotechnological research activities in India. During 2015-2016 & current year a total of
148 students have been selected in this fellowship.
Training Programmes: Department is providing support for organization of short term specialized
training programmes for upgrading skills of mid-career scientists from R & D institutions and
faculty involved in undergraduate and postgraduate teaching in multidisciplinary areas of
biotechnology. A total of 35 proposals have been recommended for financial support during the
period. Department of Biotechnology is supporting Biotech Industrial Training Programme (BITP)
for providing hands-on training for six months to fresh B.E./B.Tech./M.Sc./M.Tech. students in
biotechnology. During the period 1127 students have been placed in trainer companies under this
program. Department has created special provision in the existing HRD schemes namely DBT-RA
programme, BITP programme and Entrepreneurship development progarmme for the students/
candidates from the North Eastern Region of the country. Several students and entrepreneurs have
been benefited under these programs.
Awards/Fellowships: Rapid Grant for Young Investigators (RGYI) program fosters creative research
in various fields of biotechnology (Medical, Agriculture, Animal Biotech, Environment and Industry
etc.) to enhance early career development of young investigators below 40 years of age. The
programme aims to provide first grant to establish the lab and initiate research in the frontier areas
of biotechnology.
21.2 The Ramalingaswami Re-entry Fellowship was conceived in the year 2006-07 with the idea of
encouraging scientists (Indian Nationals) working outside the country, and who would like to return to

20
the home country to pursue their research interests in life sciences, biotechnology and other related areas.
So far 202 candidates have returned to the country to join this program.
21.3 "Energy Biosciences Overseas Fellowship" is a re-entry scheme for scientists of Indian origin who
are working outside the country in the field of Energy Biosciences. Over the past few years since 2009,
ten awardees with diverse expertise have returned to India and are working with the DBT Bioenergy
Centers, IISERs, IITs and other institutes.
21.4 Recently, Bioenergy Awards for Cutting Edge Research 'B-ACER' launched for Ph.D. students and
young scientists from India to interact with American peers and helping build long term R&D linkages.
The purpose of this award is to nurture future innovators and thought leaders in Biofuel and Bioenergy.
More than 50 applications received from young scientists and students working in Bioenergy related area.
21.5 The Department initiated Tata Innovation Fellowship program in 2006 to reward the scientists
engaged in innovation and in the pursuit of path breaking solutions to major challenges, interdisciplinary
work and an emphasis on translational research in life sciences, agriculture, biomedical science and
related areas of biotechnology. During the period (2015-2017) 10 scientists have been awarded Tata
Innovation Fellowship in the areas of Medical Biotechnology, Agricultural Biotechnology and Environmental
Biotechnology.
21.6 The W ellcome Trust/DBT India Alliance (India Alliance) was set up in 2008-09 as a 10-year £160
Million equally co-funded programme between the Wellcome Trust, UK and the Department of
Biotechnology, Government of India. By November 2016, India Alliance has made 254 awards at 79
different institutions across India.
21.7 In an attempt to enhance the participation of Women Scientists in Biotechnology Research, the
Department of Biotechnology launched a Biotechnology Career Advancement and Re-orientation Programme
(Bio-CARe) for women Scientists. The programme is mainly for Career Development of employed/
unemployed women Scientists upto 55 years of age for whom it is the first extramural research grant.
4 calls have been announced so far and 323 (113 Employed and 101 Unemployed) women Scientists have
been supported under the Bio-CARe scheme. The achievement of the schemes includes 90 publications,
04 patent and regular job for 11 women scientists during the Bio-CARE projects.
21.8 The Committee appreciates the effort being made by the Department in strengthening and
creation of infrastructure across the country in biotechnology sector, which provides immense
opportunity for promoting innovative research and training and capacity building. The Committee
is of the view that state-of-art infrastructure provides opportunities for Human Resource
Development and employment but in the absence of the efficient human resources, the very
purpose of putting state-of-art infrastructure gets defeated. The major challenge, therefore, is
the availability of adequate trained personnel to manage this infrastructure and the Committee
observes that Department in partnership with the Skill Development Councils is addressing the
issue. The Committee feels that infrastructure in itself can only provide the conducive atmosphere
to work in. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take all necessary
measures to ensure that additional requirement of adequate trained personnel is made available
and the infrastructure created is utilised optimally.

surveillance for the highly contagious and ravaging diseases so that forecasting model on
disease outbreaks in the region can be developed for a formidable defense to guard the
territories.
(x) A major collaborative research programme on Chemical Ecology of North Eastern Region
has been initiated involving scientists from reputed national institutions (National Centre for
Biological Sciences (NCBS), Indian Institute of Science (IISc), University of Agricultural
Sciences (UAS), and NER institutions.
(xi) A major network project involving five institutes from NER and DDRC/THSTI-Faridabad
has been launched on harnessing the traditional herbal medicines of NER for developing
novel therapeutic strategies for metabolic syndrome.
(xii) New initiatives launched in this year include network programmes on biodiversity of aromatic
rice strains of NER and improvement in their yield and aromatic content (Joha and Black
Rice); biodiversity of banana and its pathogens in NER and to develop nutritionally fortified
and pathogen-resistant banana strains. In the animal biotechnology area, a collaborative
programmes on Duck improvement of duck productivity has been initiated; brain storming
for detection and control of diseases in both freshwater and marine/brackish water fish, and
molecular characterization and conservation of ornamental fish of NER has been organized
in Tripura.
(xiii) In the h uman healthcare sector, new initiatives in the area of Multi-Drug Resistant Tuberculosis
(MDR-TB) in NER, its molecular characterization and advanced diagnostics, and instituting
its control in association with various NER and other institutions has been intiated. A
component on detection and characterization of various species of lung fluke Paragonimus
prevalent in NER, and its intermediate hosts has also been included with the TB programme
in NER.DBT has an autonomous institutions "Institute of Bioresources and Sustainable
Development (IBSD)" at Imphal and its regional centre in Gangtok, Sikkim.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS — AT A  GLANCE
FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE OF THE DEPARTMENT DURING THE 12TH FIVE YEAR PLAN:
The Committee notes that the Department of Biotechnology had proposed a budgetary
allocation of ````` 18000.00 cr. for the entire 12th Five Year Plan (2012-17) whereas the Department
got approval of only ````` 7876.8 crore as allocation which is less than 50 per cent. The Committee
is perturbed to note that against the approved budgetary allocation of ````` 7876.8 crore for the
entire period of 12th Five Year Plan, the Department of Biotechnology has actually received
````` 7497.00 crore (at RE stage) during the Plan period. The Committee is of the considered view
that the basic concept of a Five Year Plan is to formulate long gestation schemes/projects by
drawing long-term and mid-term projections. However, if the strategic policy interventions
envisaged are not adequately funded, negative impact on the successful execution of schemes/
projects is inevitable. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Department should
sensitise the concerned Ministry/Department of the Government of India about the higher
financial requirements of the Department more vigorously so as to enable it to smoothly discharge
its mandate. (Para 3.2)
The Committee further expresses its unhappiness to notes that the utilization capacity of
the Department has continuously gone down from 99.19 percent in 2013-14 to 96.36 percent,
95.67 percent and 85.49 percent in 2014-15, 2015-16 and 2016-17 (as on 14th February, 2017)
respectively. The Department's performance of utilising 99.19 percent of the total allocation in
2013-14 is indicative of the capabilities of optimally utilising the resources made available to it.
However, the Department appears to have failed to rise to its true potential and could spend only
85.49 percent of the allocated resources during 2016-17 till 14.02.2017. The Committee, therefore,
feels that the Department should have been more prudent in optimally utilising the funds made
available to it for the year 2016-17. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Department
to review its financial performance during 2016-17 and identify the shortfalls responsible for
underutilisation so as to avoid its recurrence in future and revisit its scheme of allocation of
funds under the various schemes/programmes/projects to make them more result oriented.
(Para 3.3)
BUDGET ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2017-18
The Committee hopes that the Department would utilise the budgetary allocation of
````` 2222.11 crore in 2017-18 optimally and ensure that the targets envisioned for the year
2017-18 in the Action Plan would be achieved in a time-frame fixed by the Department. The
Committee is of the considered view that timely completion of the targets/objectives will not only
help the Department to improve its performance both physically as well as financially but also
helping cut down the overhead costs. Thus, the Committee recommends the Department to
monitor the time frame for the envisaged targets and keep a continuous vigil with the help of
a robust internal monitoring mechanism so as to ensure that the fixed timelines are met and
the budgetary support provided for the purpose is utilised judiciously and optimally. (Para 4.3)

and impress upon them and seek the requisite budgetary allocations at RE stage so that the

while allocating or making financial allocation in favour of the scientific Departments/Ministries
should also consider that our scientific organisations deserve a lot more financial backing of the

under the Scheme. The Committee feels that the financial performance of the Department is not
very heartening. The under-utilisation of the budgetary allocation does not speak well about the

when the budget allocation has been increased at RE stage. The Committee strongly feels that

RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT
The Committee notes that during the period (2015-2017), 5724 proposals were received, out
of which only 542 (9.46%) proposals/projects have been funded so far. (Para 7.1)
BASIC RESEARCH
The Committee is of the view that making potable water available to our citizens is one of
the biggest challenges facing our country. The Committee feels that the Department of

31
Biotechnology has the potential to devise a technology to convert the filthiest of the water into
potable water. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should include
developing technologies for extracting safe drinking water from available water resources to
lessen the problem of drinking water in the country. (Para 8.2)
AGRICULTURE AND ALLIED AREAS:
CROP BIOTECHNOLOGY
The Committee appreciates the achievement realised by the Department in the field of crop
biotechnology. The Committee is of the view that agriculture, alongwith its allied sectors, is the
largest livelihood activity in our country and it is the need of the hour that we all should work
in tandem to improve our crops productivity with the help of technological advancements and
sustainable technologies by establishing a dissemination network so that the innovations reach
the last point. (Para 9.2)
The Committee also feels that out of box thinking is required to tap the potential lying in
our agricultural activities. The Committee recommends the Department to take necessary steps
in the direction of untapped potential with the help of its biotechnological strategic interventions
so as to address the issues of not only the crops productivity but also for mitigation of post
harvest loss and enhancing the nutritional value as well. (Para 9.3)
ANIMAL HEALTH
The Committee notes the activities undertaken by the Department in the field of animal
biotechnology and animal health. The Committee, nonetheless, is of the opinion that the rate of
commercialisation of the technologies developed by the Department is not very encouraging and
it reflects that the technologies so developed by the Department either are not as per the
requirements of the industry or there may be flaws in the technologies restricting their
commercialisation. Hence, the Committee desires the Department to take market driven research
activities so that the technologies developed by it are well received by the industry.
(Para 11.2)
The Committee also feels that the Department needs to augment its research activities in
the direction of disease resistance in our indigenous livestock. The Committee, therefore,
recommends the Department to take necessary action in these directions. (Para 11.3)
The Committee is further of the view that the Department should also adopt more focused
approach towards increasing the productivity of the indigenous varieties of cows in the country;
establishment of sperm banks so as to make available hybrid indigenous sperm of high quality
and standards; etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take
necessary action in this regard. (Para 11.4)
AQUACULTURE AND MARINE BIOTECHNOLOGY
The Committee notes that India has a coastline of over 8000 kms. and ranks 2nd in global
fish production, inland capture and aquaculture. The Committee, however , feels that sustainable

32
productivity and management has been a concern area where the Department of Biotechnology
needs to take the required strategic policy interventions. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Department should take necessary biotechnological measures to address the issues of
sustainable productivity and management. (Para 12.2)
The Committee is also of the opinion that health of the aquatic animal predominantly
depends on the health of the aquaculture ecosystem. Thus, development of healthy brood stock
of all cultivable fin and shell fishes assumes greater importance and the Committee feels that
the Department of Biotechnology can play a crucial role on this count. The Committee, therefore,
recommends the Department to take necessary strategic measures to develop high health brood
stock. (Para 12.3)
The Committee is of the opinion that the biological diversity of the marine resources along
the Indian coast in the form of creeks, estuaries, deep seas and continental shelf offer enormous
scope for the discovery of novel products and processes which have application in biomass and
food production, production of polymers, biocatalysts, biomedical products, and organics;
bioremediation and biomining etc. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the Department
should work out a roadmap for the purpose and put earnest efforts in this direction. The
Committee is hopeful that with the help of right policy interventions, the Department can write
a new chapter of biotechnological advancements in the field of aquaculture and marine bio-
technology. (Para 12.4)
MEDICINAL AND AROMATIC PLANTS
The Committee takes note of the various activities undertaken under Medicinal and Aromatic
Plants. The Committee observes that the Department has been supporting the salient aspects of
the Indian medicine system through its research activities. The Committee, however, feels that
the Department has to keep pace with the increasing attention about the medicinal and aromatic
plants among the urban population and take necessary measures to tap the unlimited potential
of these plants with the help of its biotechnological capabilities. (Para 13.2)
MISSION INNOV ATION - ACCELERATING THE CLEAN ENERGY REVOLUTION
The Committee notes the work done so far by the Department in the direction of biofuels.
However, lot more is yet to be achieved on this count. The Committee hopes that the Department,
along with other related agencies of the Government, will continue its concerted efforts and will
work in tandem to realise the targets set for biofuels. (Para 14.2)
The Committee is of the view that the Department should also chalk out a policy initiative
and set up Bioenergy based incubation centres across the country so as to provide a platform to
have interface between academia and industry. If required, the Department should seek budgetary
support for the purpose at RE stage. The Committee also recommends that the Department
should focus on nurturing start-ups in this direction. (Para 14.3)

33
NANOBIOTECHNOLOGY
The Committee is of the view that the application of nanotechnology can play a very
important and crucial role in the areas of agriculture, health, food, environment, etc. The
Committee feels that the Department should continue its activities in this direction and also
explore the possibilities to address the challenges posed to our agriculture, health, food and
environment with the help of advancement in the field of the nanotechnology. (Para 15.2)
MEDICAL BIOTECHNOLOGY AND RELATED AREAS:
INFECTIOUS DISEASES
The Committee is of the opinion that a diagnostic test kit for TB patients is the need of
the hour so as to enable early detection of TB. The Committee also feels that the Department
should in coordination with Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and ICMR devise innovative
technologies for the purpose. (Para 16.3)
The Committee is also of the view that the Department should undertake an awareness
campaign to popularise its technological advancements and sensitise all the State Governments
as well as medical colleges about the diagnosis and clinical symptomatic diagnosis of TB so as to
provide an important breakthrough in the early detection of the disease. (Para 16.4)
The Committee expresses concerns on the issue of mosquito breeding which appears to have
gone out of control. The Committee is of the view that the Department of Biotechnology should
play a significant role by devising technology to keep the mosquito population under control and
should examine the genda flower like pyrethrum for the purpose. Similarly, the Department
should take research work on pheromone traps for the female mosquito. (Para 16.5)
BIODESIGN PROGRAMME
The Committee notes the scientific improvements brought with the support of its research
activities in the field of medical biotechnology and related areas. The Committee hopes that the
Department would continue its focus on this sector and further strengthen its activities in the
areas of human genome research, vaccines, infectious, chronic disease biology, stem cells &
regenerative medicine and the biodesign programmes. (Para 17.2)
FOOD AND NUTRITION
The Committee takes note of the activities of the Department in the direction of Food and
Nutrition. The Committee, however, is of the view that the Department should further intensify
its activities to address the issue of Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) so as to tackle the stunting
in the children of our country which can lead to developmental problems. The Committee would
also like to be apprised of the status of the approval of FSSAI to the formulation consisting of
a mix of seven minerals and thirteen vitamins in a sachet aimed for treatment of severely
malnourished children. (Para 18.3)
The Committee also recommends that the Department should publicise its demonstration
unit developed by IIT, Kharagpur to the various states of the country and sentise and encourage

34
them to make use of the technology in their respective states to combat Severe Acute Malnutrition
(SAM). (Para 18.4)
The Committee is also of the view that the Department should in co-ordination with the
FSSAI take necessary action in the direction of making oil fortification mandatory so as to retain
the its nutritional value. (Para 18.5)
BIOTECHNOLOGY FOR SOCIETAL DEVELOPMENT
The Committee is of the considered opinion that with the help of right technological
interventions, we can bring the marginalised sections of our society into the mainstream and
make them more productive for the overall growth of the country. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department should further intensify its activities in the directions of
societal development and take necessary steps for creating platform for self-employment generation
in the industrially backward areas of the country. (Para 19.2)
The Committee is of the view that the Department of Biotechnology can play a very important
role to address the issue of clean drinking water with the help of its technological advancements.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should chalk out a roadmap for the
purpose and further strengthen its activities in this direction. (Para 19.3)
INDUSTRIAL AND ENTREPRENEURSHIP DEVELOPMENT
The Committee observes that the Department could not optimally utilise the allocation
made for 'Industrial and Entrepreneurship Development Scheme' during the years 2014-15 and
2015-16. The Committee is of the view that the Department needs to monitor its schemes
periodically and recommends that the Department should devise a monitoring mechanism whereby
all its schemes are periodically monitored and underutilization of funds is avoided.
(Para 20.10)
The Committee takes note of the activities contemplated by the Department for the year
2017-18 and hopes that the envisioned objectives of the Department would be realized with the
help of concerted and earnest strategic steps. (Para 20.11)
The Committee believes that the Department plays an instrumental and pivotal role in the
areas of transfer of technology, licensing, validation and in creation of infrastructure for
commercialisation of technologies. Also, it is essential for the Department to augment effective
engagements so as to trigger, nurture and sustain bio-entrepreneurship by creating the required
strategic policy interventions. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department
should take necessary action in the matter and also chalk out a strategic roadmap for setting
up technology development centres, incubator facilities, etc. across the country for our aspiring
entrepreneurs to prosper by creating sustainable rural industrialisation in the field of biotechnology.
(Para 20.12)

HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT
The Committee appreciates the effort being made by the Department in strengthening and
creation of infrastructure across the country in biotechnology sector, which provides immense
opportunity for promoting innovative research and training and capacity building. The Committee
is of the view that state-of-art infrastructure provides opportunities for Human Resource
Development and employment but in the absence of the efficient human resources, the very
purpose of putting state-of-art infrastructure gets defeated. The major challenge, therefore, is
the availability of adequate trained personnel to manage this infrastructure and the Committee
observes that Department in partnership with the Skill Development Councils is addressing the
issue. The Committee feels that infrastructure in itself can only provide the conducive atmosphere
to work in. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should take all necessary
measures to ensure that additional requirement of adequate trained personnel is made available
and the infrastructure created is utilised optimally. (Para 21.8)

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
The Ministry of Science and Technology was established in 1971 to formulate and implement Science
and Technology policies, identify, and promote “frontline” research in science and technology infrastructure.
The Ministry has three Departments, namely Department of Science and Technology, Department of
Biotechnology and Department of Scientific and Industrial Research. Through Department of Science and
Technology, the Ministry coordinates intra-governmental and international cooperation and provides funding
for domestic institutions and research programs. The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research is a
technology transfer organization, and the Department of Biotechnology, runs a number of developmental
laboratories.
2. The following constitute the mandate of DST:-
z Formulation of policy statements and guidelines on Science and Technology (S&T);
z Promotion of new areas of scientific research;
z Co-ordination of inter-Departmental S&T efforts;
z Support basic and applied research in universities and other institutions;
z International S&T Co-operation;
z Support high quality research in autonomous bodies where specialisation ranges from advanced
medical research materials to astronomy;
z Catalysing S&T interaction in societal programmes, and entrepreneurship development;
z Science popularisation, communication and S&T Management Information System;
z Promotion of Commercialisation of indigenous technology;
z Support to technology development programmes, technology information and assessment;
and
z Providing services in the areas of:
(i) Surveying & Mapping;
(ii) T echnology Development and Application
3. OBJECTIVES
Main objectives of the Department of Science and Technology are as follows:
(a) Formulation of Policies relating to Science and Technology;
(b) Strengthening basic research and Expanding R&D base-Human capacity;
(c) Strengthening Basic research and Expanding R&D base-Institutional Capacity;
(d) Implementing Technology Development Programmes: from R&D to Commercialisation;
(e) Societal interventions of Science & Technology; and
(f) International Science & Technology Co-operation

2
4. ORGANISATION
4.1 The Department of Science and Technology is the nodal Department of the Ministry of Science and
Technology. Broadly, the organisational set up of the Department has been divided into Autonomous Institutes,
Scientific Groups, Technology Development Board and Scientific Services besides the Administration and
Integrated Finance divisions. There are 19 Autonomous Institutions and 5 Science/Engineering Professional
bodies which are working in diverse areas for the promotion of Science and Technology. In addition, one
new autonomous body viz. National Centre for Molecular Material Research, Thiruvanathapuram has been
recently set up and National Innovation Foundation, Ahmedabad which was earlier a ‘Corpus Funded’
Financial Institute has been taken over by the Department as fully funded autonomous Research Institute.
The Scientific Groups inter-alia consists of the Science & Engineering Research Council (SERC), National
Council for Science and Technology Communication (NSCTC), National Resources Data Management
System (NRDMS), International Division, National Entrepreneurship Board (NEB), National Science and
Technology Management Information System (NSTMIS). The Scientific Services have two subordinate
offices, namely, National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation (NATMO) and Survey of India (SoI)
under their administrative control.
4.2 The detailed budget allocation of the Department of Science and Technology for the year 2017-18
was considered by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology,
Environment and Forests in its meeting held on the 14

12.2 Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research, Bengaluru
Established in the year 1989, Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research (JNCASR)
is an autonomous institution of the Department of Science and Technology DST. The Centre is also a
Deemed University. Over the last 27 years, the Centre has emerged as a leading institution of excellence in
research and training in frontier areas of materials science, chemistry, physics, biology, geodynamics and
theoretical sciences and engineering mechanics. Large number of publications and patents from the Centre
reveal its excellence in research. The Centre has carved out a special place for itself owing to its unique
profile, with the co-existence of fundamental research and translational activities across the disciplines.
12.3 Many landmark research publications and inventions have emerged from the various research activities
at the Centre. The Centre has been recently accredited by NAAC with A++ grade. Currently 305 students
are engaged in research in the Centre pursuing various academic programmes including 232 for Ph.D, 55
for Integrated Ph.D, 17 for M.S. Engg. and 1 for Postgraduate Diploma in Materials Science. During the
current year, 23 patent applications were filed and 10 patents were registered. JNC’s first start up viz.
Sankhya Sutra Labs Pvt. Ltd has commenced its activities and a few proposals for new start-ups are under
consideration. JNCASR has a vibrant science outreach programme and continues its involvement in reaching
the basic science to the children particularly in rural areas of India. The Centre is in the process of embarking
into newer areas such as computational biology, synthetic biology, energy, new materials and several other
emerging topics in the science and engineering, in the coming year. The Committee visited a few laboratories
and facilities at the Centre and also interacted with the students and research scholars regarding the research
activities and Science Outreach Programmes of the Centre.
12.4 During the meeting of the Committee with the representatives of JNCASR, the Committee was
informed that JNCASR planned to have significant impact on global scientific activity and be a part of
national scientific and technology missions. The diverse range of disciplines defines the context in developing
a roadmap, by choosing and investing in subject areas which will have substantial and wide-ranging impact.
In addition to consolidating its strength in the existing core areas, to grow by recruiting faculty in the areas
of Materials for Energy and Environment, Computational Science and Applied Mathematics, Chemical Biology
and Soft Chemistry, Nonequiilbrium Statistical Mechanics relevant to soft matter and physical biology, Earth
Sciences and Fluid dynamics.
12.5 The Committee desired to know about major financial constraints faced by the centre in achieving its
goals in terms of funding and facilities. The Committee was informed that the DST has been supporting the
Centre with grant-in-aid in the range of ` 40-50 Crore annually, during the past four years. In addition, a
Technical Research Centre (TRC) for pursuing translational research activities has been funded by the DST,
Government of India with a total outlay of ` 96.82 Crore for a period of five years from 2015-16. Extramural

17
competitive grants have been received by the Centre for various projects and contributions from the government
funding agencies, industry and other sources. In order to expand in the newer areas of science, translate the
research results to the industry and academia and foster collaborations, the Centre needs to acquire and
upgrade the laboratories as also recruit outstanding faculty members. In order to achieve this, the Centre
needs enhanced budgetary support for which it has made request to the DST. Representatives of JNCASR
also brought out that the budget outlay of the Centre had not increased over the years and stressed the need
for additional grants to the tune of ` 100 Crore to develop their new campus wherein they planned to initiate
research in new areas of science.
12.6 The Committee appreciates the efforts of research scholars, faculty and the other authorities
of JNCASR. The Committee recommends that JNCASR community should leave no stone unturned
to strengthen their efforts and capabilities to reach greater heights in the frontier areas of science
and Technology and to initiate research in new areas of science and to reach the next level of
performance and excellence, with commitment to societal issues so that the results of science

of the request of JNCASR for increase of their budget outlay which has not increased since the last

12.7 The Committee also notes the future expansion plans of the Centre to construct the necessary

13. RAMAN  RESEARCH  INSTITUTE
13.1 The Committee visited the Raman Research Institute on the 29
th August, 2016. The Committee initially
visited the Science Museum and a few laboratories and facilities at the Institute and also interacted with the

13.2 RRI is an icon that symbolizes and represents the heritage of Indian physicist and Nobel Laureate Sir
C V Raman, continuing his legacy and style of qualitatively impactful research that earns the nation a
respectable place. The Institute preserves the inspirational spirit of this stalwart of our scientific cultural
history.
13.3 The mandate of the Institute is basic research with focus in niche fields of astronomy and astrophysics,
quantum atom optics, quantum information, soft condensed matter and theoretical physics. The research
activities include work in Chemistry, Liquid Crystals, Physics in Biology.
13.4 The Committee was informed that the Institute partners Harvard, MIT and institutions in the US,
Australia and New Zealand in building the precursor Radio Telescopes for the Square Kilometer Array
(SKA), which is a megaproject of the nation.  RRI designed and built in India all of the high technology
Digital Receivers for this international telescope and installed the receivers in the SKA site. RRI works to

18
grow a cohesive younger generation that will continue the country’s leadership in this futuristic international
research by building in Indian soil the SWAN project, which is a radio telescope north of Bengaluru engaged
in research in the emerging field of time domain radio astronomy involving university students.
13.5 RRI designed and developed in-house an X-ray polarimeter called POLIX to shed light on cosmic
X-ray sources. POLIX is poised to be the first dedicated X-ray polarimetry mission in the world to measure
X-ray polarisation in about 50 bright X-ray sources. This X-ray astronomy project is in close collaboration
with the Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO).
13.6 During the meeting, the Committee desired to know the future vision of the Institute. In response
thereto, the Committee was informed that the Institute’s emphasis was on continued research that
would require substantial engineering developments to enable the science, so that multitudes of visiting
students, PhD students, research assistants and associates would be empowered to design, develop,
build, and commission complex systems that work in the real world, and inherit confidence and
expertise.
13.7 The Committee also desired the know about the funding pattern of the Institute and financial constraints,
if any, faced by the Institute. The Committee informed that the Institute is dependent on funding from
Government of India, through the Department of Science and Technology, Annually, Department of Science
and Technology releases about `36 crores as grant-in-aid. It was also informed that some additional funding
would greatly help the Institute to sustain excellence in experimental research, which is the culture and
hallmark and uniqueness of the historical institution, and the legacy of its Founder.
13.8 The Committee was also informed that as one of the examples of societal relevance, the electrochemistry
laboratory of Raman Research Institute has invented an impedance based ‘Hand-held milk purity testing
device’ to detect the so called ‘synthetic milk adulteration’.
13.9 The Committee appreciates the free-spirited research that is undertaken at Raman Research
Institute which has resulted in improved understanding of the fundamental laws and behaviour of
nature to take necessary action. The Committee also commends the Institute for having invented
the Hand-held milk purity testing device and would request the Department of Science and Technology
to take necessary action to commercialise the device at the earliest so that the invention could
benefit the common people of the country.

th October, 2016. During

15. MEGA  FACILITIES  FOR  BASIC  RESEARCH
15.1 The Mega Facilities for Basic Research Programme, or the Mega Science Programme, as it is
popularly known, aims at creating Mega Science facilities and launch Mega Science projects in and out of
the country to improve access to such state-of-the-art facilities for the Indian scientific community,
especially from the academic sector. Such projects, being technically extremely complex and requiring
huge funds and other resources, are mostly, and naturally, multi-agency, multi-institutional and most
often, international in character. Most of the projects currently under implementation under this programme
in the areas of nuclear physics, high energy physics, astronomy and astrophysics etc., have been jointly
funded and overseen by the Department of Science and Technology (DST) and the Department of Atomic
Energy (DAE). DST and DAE have a long-standing Memorandum of Understanding on joint funding,
implementation and monitoring of such projects. Several important developments took place during the
year under this Programme.
15.2 The M ega Facilities for  the Basic Research Programme has twin objectives:
(i) to enable  Indian  scientists to participate in building very large international facilities which are
manifestly multinational efforts and gain access to the same for scientific studies, and
(ii) to create  some  facilities  of  international  standards  in the country. India’s participation in the
Large Hadron Collider (LHC), FAIR, the Thirty Metre Telescope (TMT), etc. falls in this
category.
15.3 The Department was asked about the performance of Mega Facilities for Basic Research Programme
in last 3 years and steps taken for creating Mega facilities. It was replied that projects under the “Mega
Facilities for Basic Research Programme” are such projects that not only require huge financial resources
but also sophisticated scientific knowledge at the very frontiers. In fact, such projects also push the global
technology frontiers. Such projects are set up at the best possible locations in the world and with the best
possible global know-how.

20
15.4 The Committee was informed that India’s participation in such projects worldwide is certainly helping
in setting up a few such projects for basic research in the country. For example, the India-based Neutrino
Observatory (INO) project in Tamil Nadu will use Resistive Plate Chambers as the detector element which
has been pioneered by CERN, Geneva and Indian scientists have participated in this development there as a
part of the CERN-India Collaboration. Participation of Indian scientists in neutrino experiments at Fermilab
will also help in doing science at INO. Indian scientists have made significant contributions towards the
LHC Computing Grid and established two Tier 2 Grid Computing facilities in the country for analyzing the
CERN data. This has initiated Grid Computing activities in the country, which has much wider scope of
application. The segmented mirror technology that is being learnt by the Indian astronomy community will
pave the way for establishing a large (8-10 m class) optical telescope at a suitable site in the Himalayas at an
appropriate time in future.
15.5 Responding to the query of the Committee about collaboration of DST and Department of Atomic
Energy, it was informed that creation of such huge research infrastructures in the country is a multi-agency
task. DAE and DST have shown excellent cooperation and coordination in creating such infrastructure in
the country. Most of the national and international projects planned for the XII Plan period had been initiated
by the Department.
15.6 The Committee desired to know the progress made in the areas identified by the Department in
collaboration with the Department of Atomic Energy for building effective partnership in creating mega
facilities. It was informed that the ongoing projects were in the areas of nuclear physics, high energy
physics, astronomy and astrophysics, macromolecular crystallography and materials science. Scientific
deliberations were in progress for new initiatives under Mega Facilities for Basic Research programme
which included establishing a new generation synchrotron radiation source facility in the country. For
identifying other areas, a Vision meeting was planned shortly.
15.7 The Committee commends the infrastructure developed under Mega Facilities for Basic
Research in partnership with national and international agencies particularly with the Department
of Atomic Energy and recommends that adequate budgetary provision should be made for marching
ahead in avant-garde science.
Financial Performance
15.8  Budgetary allocation to ‘Mega facilities for Basic Research’ was reduced from ` 120.00 Crore in
B.E. 2016-17 to ` 80.00 Crore in R.E. 2016-17. The Committee desired to know the reason behind increase
of allocation to the tune of ` 10.00 Crore over BE-2017-18 allocation despite the fact that last year only
` 51.29 Crore were utilised by January, 2017. In response thereto, the Department has informed that an
amount of ` 40.00 Crore had been included in Plan B.E. allocation 2016-17 for payment of DST’s share
(50%) towards India’s Associate Membership of the European Organization of Nuclear Research (CERN),
Geneva. India obtained the Associate Member status w.e.f. 16.01.2017 only. The Department has informed
that during the end of financial year 2016-17 India will have to make a payment of about ` 20.00 Crore only,
thereby reducing the DST’s requirement of funds on this count to approximately ` 10 Crore This has led to
a reduction of ` 30 Crore at the R.E. 2016-17 stage.
15.9 Explaining the delay in time bound creation of Mega facilities, it has been informed that the Mega
Facilities for Basic Research Head also included expenditure towards DST’s share for the Thirty Metre
Telescope (TMT) project at Mauna Kea, Hawaii, USA. Work on this project got slowed down because of

21
Court Orders in Hawaii to obtain Permits for the Mauna Kea site afresh. While this was being done, the
international consortium leading that project had identified an alternate site at La Palma in Canary Islands of
Spain for the project, in case the Mauna Kea site did not become available within a reasonable time-frame. In
the meantime, design, prototyping and testing of telescope components were going on in full swing. These
developments led to a smaller expenditure for this project during the year, thereby reducing the R.E.
2016-17 figure by another ` 10.00 Crore.
15.10 The Department has informed that with the Associate Membership of CERN now in place, DST’s
expenditure towards this will be about ` 40 Crore next year as against to approximately ` 10 Crore this year.
Firm decision on the site of TMT (either Mauna Kea or La Palma) will be in place during 2017-18 and
expenditure on this project will pick up. An additional amount of ` 20.00 Crore is expected on this count. In total
B.E. 2017-18 allocations for TMT comes to 13.00 Crore The National Large Solar Telescope (NLST) project
is expected to be sanctioned during 2017-18. The total cost of this project is ` 496 Crore and some initial funds
will also have to be granted for this. The Department has assured that allocation will be gainfully utilised.
15.11 When the Committee desired to know the benefits of becoming an associate Members of CERN, it
was informed that as an Associate Member State of CERN, India will be a part of the huge scientific and
technological endeavour. It will be the start of a renewed and stronger collaboration between CERN and
India, which will be an advantageous situation for both the parties. Indian scientists will be able to participate
in the activities at CERN in a big way. India will be able to participate in CERN Council meetings, related
scientific discussions and will have say in decision-making on important policy issues. There will be enhanced
level of participation in CERN activities by India which will ensure more opportunities for Indian scientists,
research students, technical staff and industry. Indian industry will be allowed to bid for CERN contracts
thus opening up opportunities for industrial collaboration in areas of advanced technologies.Technology
transfer will also be feasible now with Indian Industry. India will have higher Discovery potential in fundamental
science and technology. There will be enhanced level of human resource development programmes like
Summer training programs at CERN, Exchange programs, Periodic visits of eminent scientists from CERN
to India, Outreach activities, etc. The experience to be gained in the course of the collaborative effort will
definitely help the Indian scientists, technologists and engineers to develop competence and expertise for
indigenous development of important hi-tech technologies in future.
15.12 The Committee congratulates the Department for attaining the associate membership of the
European Organisation for Nuclear Research (CERN), Geneva and hopes that it will help India
further advance in avant-garde science. The Committee also hopes that with the finalization of the
process of India becoming an Associate Member of CERN, the funds under Mega Facilities for Basic
Research would now be optimally utilised by Department of Science and Technology and desired
output will be achieved.
16. NATIONAL  SUPERCOMPUTING  FACILITY  AND  CAPACITY  BUILDING
16.1 National Supercomputing Mission is driven by the aim to consolidate and build synergy in various
ongoing efforts in supercomputing across the country.
16.2 Some of the mission oriented departments such as Defence and Research Development Organisation
(DRDO), DAE and other few leading academic institutions were involved in the use of supercomputers.
However, in the recent times, many more departments and research laboratories in government, financial
sector, telecom  industry, e-governance, Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI), education, and
intelligence agencies have also come into the fold of users of supercomputers. Private sectors such as

22
pharmaceutical industry, automotive industry, online gaming industry, entertainment industry, online services
with Indian language contents have also joined the field.
16.3 Supercomputing has potential applications in the fields of climate modeling, weather prediction,
engineering including CFD, CSM, CEM, Agriculture Research and Education, Computational Biology, Materials
and Chemicals., Molecular Dynamics, Atomic energy simulations, Security and defence applications, financial
and Big Data Analytics. Additionally, it can also be used in the disaster simulations and management, discoveries
beyond Earth (Astrophysics) and Information Repositories and Government Information Systems.
16.4 The major objectives of the Mission are:-
(i) Make India a world leader in High Performance Computing (HPC) and to enhance the national
capability in solving grand challenge problems of national and global relevance;
(ii) Empower scientists and researchers with state-of-the-art compute facilities for their cutting-
edge research in respective Domains;
(iii) Reduce redundancies and avoiding duplication of efforts and investments; and
(iv) Attain global competitiveness and self-reliance in HPC.
16.5 The Mission is partnered by the DST, the Department of Electronics and Information Technology in
consultation with the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru and Centre for Development of Advance Computing
(C-DAC), Pune. These organisations are preparing the strategies for implementing the Programme. In view of the
inter-ministerial nature of the proposed mission, National Supercomputing Mission follows six principles namely
ONE Mission, ONE Goal, Mission First, Centralised Planning, Decentralised Implementation, Clear Division of
Roles, Responsibilities and Costs, Harmonisation, Coordination and Sharing; and Federated Governance Structure.
16.6 Financial aspects
Total budget allocated for the seven years for Supercomputing Mission is ` 4, 500 Crore out of which
DST will be contributing ` 2,740 Crore; whereas ` 1,760 Crore will be contributed by DeitY . The project is to
be completed within seven years. Some of the key deliverables of the project are 70+ HPC installations, HPC
Grid, Million-core cloud, development of HPC applications, 20000 HPC-aware manpower, R&D for next-
generation Exa-Scale HPC. The total cost of this seven years mission is ` 4500 Crore with following breakup.

16.9 The Committee desired to know the reason for underutilisation of funds in Super Computing Mission.
In response, it was informed by the Department that the Programme was flagged off in 2015 only. All the
