the plan layout within various sectors in the National Super Computing Mission. The second Empowerment
Board meeting was held only on 2

has delayed the release of the funds. The Department further added that ` 30.00 Crore of funds have been
now approved for release and the rest of the amount is also proposed to be released before the year end. It
was also informed that for the National Super Computing Mission was also comprising a little part of the big
data sub-programmes that will take nearly ` 20 Crore of the expenses. The Department was hopeful that in
the National Super Computing Mission, the whole Budget of ` 90.00 Crore will be spent by the end of
financial year 2016-17.
16.10 Not convinced with the reply furnished by Department of Science and Technology, the Committee
desired to know the reason behind delay in the programme. Replying to the query, the Secretary agreed that
there were some initial hiccups but the Programme was on fully on track and by 15
th August, 2017 they were
planning to release three supercomputers built in India and three super computers would be imported. In
summation, DST was working on two parallel tracks: one was to build capacity domestically as well as to
get supercomputers from international market.
16.11 The Committee observes that there has been undue delay in the operationalisation of National
Supercomputing Programme. The inordinate delay in holding of meeting of National Empowerment
Board is inexplicable as it resulted in undue delay in the operationalisation of Mission, practically
ruling out the possibility of making any significant headway for realising the Mission.
16.12 The Committee, therefore, expresses its strong displeasure that the Department has not
even been able to fully utilise funds meant for operationalisation of Supercomputing Mission and
recommends that the Department should ensure full utilisation of allocated resources and should
ask for additional funds only when it is in a position to utilise additional funds asked for by it. The
Committee is also of the considered view that the procedural aspects of the National Supercomputing
Mission could have been handled in a better way and a proactive approach should have been adopted
to get the desired result which sadly is lacking.
16.13 The Committee also finds that India was a leader in Supercomputing till 2005 but it has now
slipped down in the global ranking. The Committee is of the view that boosting indigenous efforts in
Supercomputing capability is in strategic interests of India, more so when Information Technology
capabilities of the country are recognised worldwide. The Committee recommends that considering

24
the significance of Supercomputing, the Department should make every possible effort to execute
the programme in a mission mode, with a view to avoid any delay.

18. EFFORTS  FOR  RETAINING  RESEARCH  TALENT  IN  THE  COUNTRY
18.1 The Committee desired to know the details of efforts being made by the Department for retaining
research talent in the country. The Department informed that it had taken several steps for retaining research
talent in the country such as successive increase in plan allocations, offering attractive research fellowships
like JC Bose, Ramanujan, Swarna Jayanti, implementation of schemes in priority areas like energy, water,
climate etc. The schemes are designed to identify promising and potential scientists with innovative ideas
and provide them with training and research opportunities in niche areas of basic science and engineering.

27
Ease of funding, speed of delivery of services, attractive fellowships for young researchers etc. are some of
the characteristics of the extramural research schemes. Basic research has been given additional thrust
through establishing the Science and Engineering Research Board. Young scientists received immense support
through schemes like Early Career Research Award, National Postdoctoral Fellowship etc. Special schemes
had been in operation to strengthen infrastructure for Research and Development (R&D) in Universities and
thereby improving the working conditions of the scientists. Through these initiatives the Department has
created a conducive environment for doing research and development in the country at par with international
standards.
18.2 Informing about Ramanujan Fellowship of the Department it was stated that Ramanujan Fellowship is
a targeted scheme aimed to attract highly skilled Indian researchers working overseas by providing them
attractive avenue to pursue their R&D interests in Indian institutions. A Search and Selection Committee has
evaluated the impact of the scheme. It was observed that the scheme has served its aim of providing a good
re-entry opportunity for the recipients. The awarded fellows published a number of research articles on
their scientific investigations in peer reviewed reputed journals of high impact factor. The age profile of the
Ramanujan Fellows indicates that the vast majority of the Fellows are in the early-career stage. More than
90% of Ramanujan fellows are absorbed by the Indian S&T system through permanent positions within a
period of five years. The research performance of more than two thirds of Ramanujan Fellows match their
colleagues’ in their host institutes within the specified five-year period.
18.3 In addition to the above scheme, Scientific and Engineering Research Board has approved 2-3 new
schemes in 2017-18. A Scheme is designed to tap the expertise of International Faculty/scientists including
NRI/PIO/OCI called Visiting Advanced Joint Research Faculty Scheme (V AJRA). Overseas Visiting Doctoral
Programme designed for Indian PhD students admitted in Indian institutions for gaining exposure and training
in overseas universities for a period of 12 months.
18.4 The Committee takes note of the schemes run by the Department that have resulted in
arresting brain drain of accomplished scientists to India particularly Visiting Advanced Joint Research
Scheme and Overseas Visiting Doctoral Programme and hopes that these initiatives will create
conducive environment for doing R&D in the country at par with international standards and yield
desired results.
19. POPULARISATION  OF  TECHNOLOGIES  DEVELOPED
19.1 The Committee understands that Scientific Departments of Government of India have developed
a number of technologies that are ready for commercialisation. Departments of Atomic Energy and
Space have also developed many spin off technologies which have the potential to serve the society in
a number of ways, for instance providing potable water, checking adulteration in milk, keeping the
environment clean and green and providing healthcare at affordable cost. However, the Committee is
concerned with the slow pace at which these socially useful technologies developed by various Scientific
Departments are trickling down to the targeted groups in particular and society in general. This is
primarily because Scientific Departments have not made any proactive combined effort to create a
dedicated agency and portal for popularisation of socially useful technologies and other technologies
ready for commercialisation. Though some individual efforts like Board of Radiation and Isotope
Technology (BRIT) of Department of Atomic Energy have been created but they are inadequate and are
like a drop in the Ocean.

28
19.2 The Committee is of the opinion that the pace of dissemination of fruits of technology to the
end user needs to be expedited. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Department of Science
and Technology, being the nodal department of scientific department responsible for consideration
and policy formulation, in collaboration with other scientific Departments, should consider developing
an institutional mechanism exclusively for marketing and popularization of technologies developed
by various scientific departments, so that the benefits of these technologies are actually utilised by
the people for whom those are intended.
20. UTILISATION  OF  SOCIALLY  USEFUL  TECHNOLOGIES  READY  FOR  COMMERCIAL
USE  DEVELOPED  BY  SCIENTIFIC  DEPARTMENTS  WITH  SCHEMES/PROGRAMMES
OF  MINISTRIES/DEPARTMENTS
20.1 Co-ordination and collaboration with other Ministries of Government of India is extremely
important for success of the schemes of Government. In this regard, when the Committee desired to
know about the mechanism of co-ordination with other Departments it was informed by the Department
that it was coordinating with other Ministries/Departments based on the national priorities and needs in
science and technology areas. It was further been informed by the Department that it has collaborated
with the Department of Heavy Industries on electric Mobility vehicles Research and Development. It
has also coordinated with Ministry of Railways to take up R&D projects on the requirements and needs
of Railways. The Department has informed that it is helping out the Ministry of Urban Development in
preparing a Compendium of technologies in waste management and disposal by industries. These
initiatives are decided and approved at the level of both Secretary and Minister of respective Ministries
and Departments.
20.2 The Committee welcomes the joint collaborative steps taken by DST in collaboration with
Department of Heavy Industries, Ministries of Railways and Urban Development and hopes that
these collaborations will fill the critical gaps.  The Committee is of the view that the Department
should leave no stone unturned in assisting the lead Ministries/Departments for the success of
these programmes.
20.3 The Committee feels that yet another effective way of gainfully utilizing the socially beneficial
technologies ready for commercial use could be to integrate them with the related schemes/
programmes being run by various Ministries/Departments of Government of India. All that the
Department of Science and Technology needs to do is to reach out to the concerned Ministries/
Departments and to impress upon them to integrate into their programmes/projects, these proven
technologies. For example, providing potable drinking water in rural and urban areas has turned
out to be a formidable challenge for the Ministries of Drinking water and Sanitation and Urban
Development during natural Disaster which has affected country in a big way in recent past. After
such disaster, problem of drinking water affects people in a big way. CSIR has developed Reverse
Osmosis mounted bus. This technology can be of great help to affected States facing natural disaster.
Similarly, Department of Atomic Energy has proven technology for water purification sludge
hygienisation and water desalination, which costs as less as 6 Paisa per litre. This technology can
easily be replicated at all those places facing safe potable water problems or where underground
water is contaminated with arsenic or fluoride, etc. both in urban and rural areas of the country by
getting it linked with Rural Water Mission and in the urban areas with the Urban Local Government
Bodies.

29
20.4  Similarly, Department of Science and Technology can help power deficient states with
transferring solar LED bulbs, Surya Jyoti which saves power. Milk adulteration checking technology
developed by Departments of Science and Technology and Scientific and Industrial Research can be
shared with State Governments and Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The Committee believes
that by doing so the Department would be able to disseminate socially beneficial technologies ready
for commercial use in a big way and their benefits would also easily reach to the people and the
society. This will also help the Ministry of Science and Technology earn creditability and goodwill.
20.5 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Science and Technology
being the nodal Department for Science, Technology and Innovation should act on the lines being
suggested by the Committee and initiate interaction with the concerned Ministries/Departments
to convince them of the relevance and efficacy of technologies developed by Scientific Departments
within a given time-frame. The Committee also recommends that the Department should take
all possible measures to take the technologies to the people as technology lying in the labyrinth
of laboratory is good for nothing. Its real success lies in its application for the benefit of the
poorest and the weakest.

Department should take all necessary measures to ensure early and successful implementation of
this programme.” (Para 11.13)
The Committee notes that this year also, the grounds furnished by the Department for
underutilisation of funds are not convincing. The Committee feels that underutilisation of scarce
funds by Survey of India defeats the objective of allocation of funds to scientific organisations with
high hopes of reaping their benefits for larger interest of masses. The Committee therefore
recommends that the Department must make a firm resolve and unflinching commitment to fully
utilise the resources allocated to the Department this year and accomplish the task of modernisation
of Mapping organisations. (Para 11.14)
JAW AHARLAL  NEHRU  CENTRE  FOR  ADVANCED  SCIENTIFIC  RESEARCH,  BENGALURU
The Committee appreciates the efforts of research scholars, faculty and the other authorities
of JNCASR. The Committee recommends that JNCASR community should leave no stone unturned
to strengthen their efforts and capabilities to reach greater heights in the frontier areas of science
and Technology and to initiate research in new areas of science and to reach the next level of
performance and excellence, with commitment to societal issues so that the results of science
reaches the industry as well as to the larger benefit of the society. The Committee also takes note
of the request of JNCASR for increase of their budget outlay which has not increased since the last
few years and recommends that Department of Science and Technology should consider the request
of JNCASR in terms of their own parameters so that the Centre does not face any hindrance in
undertaking its Research and Science Outreach Programmes. (Para 12.6)
The Committee also notes the future expansion plans of the Centre to construct the necessary
infrastructure on its second campus and an additional grant of ````` 100 crore for the purpose. The
Committee recommends that Department of Science and Technology should examine the proposal
of JNCASR on its merit and take a decision thereon as per the existing mechanism in the
Department. (Para 12.7)
RAMAN  RESEARCH  INSTITUTE
The Committee appreciates the free-spirited research that is undertaken at Raman Research
Institute which has resulted in improved understanding of the fundamental laws and behaviour of
nature to take necessary action. The Committee also commends the Institute for having invented
the Hand-held milk purity testing device and would request the Department of Science and Technology
to take necessary action to commercialise the device at the earliest so that the invention could
benefit the common people of the country. (Para 13.9)

33
THE  NATIONAL  ATLAS  AND  THEMATIC  MAPPING  ORGANIZATION  (NATMO)
The Committee recommends that Department of Science and Technology should look into all
the above issues that emerged during the meeting with the representatives of NATMO and take
necessary action thereon. The Committee is also of the view that NATMO must improve the quality
of its publications and ensure its availability for the readers/students at reasonable rates. Further,
if NATMO is not in a position to do the same, the Department should consider outsourcing the task
printing and distribution to the private players on royalty basis. This will not only result in some
earning for the publications in the market. (Para 14.5)
MEGA  FACILITIES  FOR  BASIC  RESEARCH
The Committee commends the infrastructure developed under Mega Facilities for Basic
Research in partnership with national and international agencies particularly with the Department
of Atomic Energy and recommends that adequate budgetary provision should be made for marching
ahead in avant-garde science. (Para 15.7)
The Committee congratulates the Department for attaining the associate membership of the
European Organisation for Nuclear Research (CERN), Geneva and hopes that it will help India
further advance in avant-garde science. The Committee also hopes that with the finalization of the
process of India becoming an Associate Member of CERN, the funds under Mega Facilities for Basic
Research would now be optimally utilised by Department of Science and Technology and desired
output will be achieved. (Para 15.12)
NATIONAL  SUPERCOMPUTING  FACILITY  AND  CAPACITY  BUILDING
The financial performance of the Programme during the last five years makes it clear that
the performance of the Programme has been extremely poor. (Para 16.8)
The Committee observes that there has been undue delay in the operationalisation of National
Supercomputing Programme. The inordinate delay in holding of meeting of National Empowerment
Board is inexplicable as it resulted in undue delay in the operationalisation of Mission, practically
ruling out the possibility of making any significant headway for realising the Mission.
(Para 16.11)
The Committee, therefore, expresses its strong displeasure that the Department has not even
been able to fully utilise funds meant for operationalisation of Supercomputing Mission and
recommends that the Department should ensure full utilisation of allocated resources and should
ask for additional funds only when it is in a position to utilise additional funds asked for by it. The
Committee is also of the considered view that the procedural aspects of the National Supercomputing
Mission could have been handled in a better way and a proactive approach should have been adopted
to get the desired result which sadly is lacking. (Para 16.12)
The Committee also finds that India was a leader in Supercomputing till 2005 but it has now
slipped down in the global ranking. The Committee is of the view that boosting indigenous efforts in
Supercomputing capability is in strategic interests of India, more so when Information Technology
capabilities of the country are recognised worldwide. The Committee recommends that considering

34
the significance of Supercomputing, the Department should make every possible effort to execute
the programme in a mission mode, with a view to avoid any delay. (Para 16.13)
THE NATIONAL MISSION ON NANO SCINECE AND TECHNOLOGY
The Committee notes with satisfaction that India holds the third rank in terms of publications
of papers on Nano science and technology/Materials area. The Committee takes note of the various
initiatives taken under the National Nano Science and Technology Programme such as thematic
projects, Nano Application and Technology Development Programme and hopes that the programme
will achieve the targets set within stipulated time. (Para 17.11)
The Committee finds that fund utilisation under the Mission has improved under the
Programme in the last three years. However, the Committee recommends that the Department
should inject the qualitative parameters in terms of utilization of resources of the National Mission
on Nano Science and Technology and set regulatory framework for Nano Science and Technology
expeditiously. (Para 17.12)
EFFORTS  FOR  RETAINING  RESEARCH  TALENT  IN  THE  COUNTRY
The Committee takes note of the schemes run by the Department that have resulted in
arresting brain drain of accomplished scientists to India particularly Visiting Advanced Joint Research
Scheme and Overseas Visiting Doctoral Programme and hopes that these initiatives will create
conducive environment for doing R&D in the country at par with international standards and yield
desired results. (Para 18.4)
POPULARISATION  OF  TECHNOLOGIES  DEVELOPED
The Committee is of the opinion that the pace of dissemination of fruits of technology to the
end user needs to be expedited. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Department of Science
and Technology, being the nodal department of scientific department responsible for consideration
and policy formulation, in collaboration with other scientific Departments, should consider developing
an institutional mechanism exclusively for marketing and popularization of technologies developed
by various scientific departments, so that the benefits of these technologies are actually utilised by
the people for whom those are intended. (Para 19.2)
UTILISATION  OF  SOCIALLY  USEFUL  TECHNOLOGIES  READY  FOR  COMMERCIAL  USE
DEVELOPED  BY  SCIENTIFIC  DEPARTMENTS  WITH  SCHEMES/PROGRAMMES
OF  MINISTRIES/DEPARTMENTS
The Committee welcomes the joint collaborative steps taken by DST in collaboration with
Department of Heavy Industries, Ministries of Railways and Urban Development and hopes that
these collaborations will fill the critical gaps.  The Committee is of the view that the Department
should leave no stone unturned in assisting the lead Ministries/Departments for the success of
these programmes. (Para 20.2)
The Committee feels that yet another effective way of gainfully utilizing the socially beneficial
technologies ready for commercial use could be to integrate them with the related schemes/
programmes being run by various Ministries/Departments of Government of India. All that the
Department of Science and Technology needs to do is to reach out to the concerned Ministries/

35
Departments and to impress upon them to integrate into their programmes/projects, these proven
technologies. For example, providing potable drinking water in rural and urban areas has turned
out to be a formidable challenge for the Ministries of Drinking water and Sanitation and Urban
Development during natural Disaster which has affected country in a big way in recent past. After
such disaster, problem of drinking water affects people in a big way. CSIR has developed Reverse
Osmosis mounted bus. This technology can be of great help to affected States facing natural disaster.
Similarly, Department of Atomic Energy has proven technology for water purification sludge
hygienisation and water desalination, which costs as less as 6 Paisa per litre. This technology can
easily be replicated at all those places facing safe potable water problems or where underground
water is contaminated with arsenic or fluoride, etc. both in urban and rural areas of the country
by getting it linked with Rural Water Mission and in the urban areas with the Urban Local
Government Bodies. (Para 20.3)
Similarly, Department of Science and Technology can help power deficient states with
transferring solar LED bulbs, Surya Jyoti which saves power. Milk adulteration checking technology
developed by Departments of Science and Technology and Scientific and Industrial Research can be
shared with State Governments and Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. The Committee believes
that by doing so the Department would be able to disseminate socially beneficial technologies ready
for commercial use in a big way and their benefits would also easily reach to the people and the
society. This will also help the Ministry of Science and Technology earn creditability and goodwill.
(Para 20.4)
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Science and Technology
being the nodal Department for Science, Technology and Innovation should act on the lines being
suggested by the Committee and initiate interaction with the concerned Ministries/Departments
to convince them of the relevance and efficacy of technologies developed by Scientific Departments
within a given time-frame. The Committee also recommends that the Department should take
all possible measures to take the technologies to the people as technology lying in the labyrinth
of laboratory is good for nothing. Its real success lies in its application for the benefit of the
poorest and the weakest. (Para 20.5)

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research is one of the three Departments of the
Ministry of Science and Technology. The mandate of Department of Scientific and Industrial Research
includes promotion of industrial research for indigenous technology promotion, development, utilisation
and transfer.
1.1 The primary endeavour of DSIR is to foster development of state-of-the-art technologies and
products through research and development (R&D), encourage industry to increase their share in
the country’s R&D expenditure, support industrial units in developing competitive technologies of
high commercial potential, catalyze faster commercialisation of laboratory-scale R&D, and strengthen
consultancy and technology management capabilities.
1.2 The DSIR has two public sector undertakings viz. National Research Development Corporation
(NRDC) and Central Electronics Ltd. (CEL) and two autonomous organizations viz. Council for
Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and Consultancy Development Centre (CDC). The
Department also provides host facilities and assistance to Asian and Pacific Centre for Transfer of
Technology (APCTT) as the focal point in the country.
1.3 The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology,
Environment and Forests considered the Demands for Grants (2017-18) of the Department of Scientific
and Industrial Research in its meeting held on 15th February, 2017.
2. FINANCIAL ACHIEVEMENTS OF THE DEPARTMENT

have proper and robust monitoring mechanism for utilising the allocated funds so that optimum

3. REQUEST & JUSTIFICATION FOR ADDITIONAL BUDGETARY ALLOCATION FOR
FY 2017-18
3.1 The Committee during its meeting held on 15th February, 2017 was informed by the Department
that against the Projected BE of ` 5751.36 cr., the Department has been allocated an amount of
` 4446.00 cr. during 2017-18. The Committee enquired from the Department how it would cope up
with the gap between the allocated amount of ` 4446.00 cr. against the projected amount of ` 5751.36
cr. for BE 2017-18.
3.2 The Department submitted before the Committee that the DSIR especially CSIR has been
under tremendous financial strain. The allocated amount of ` 4446.00 cr. does not include the 7th
Pay Commission impact which they had projected. The Government has committed that 70 percent
of it will be borne by the Government and 30 percent by the CSIR through its internal resources.
But that 70 percent component has not been included in allocated amount of ` 4446.00 cr. for BE
2017-18. The Department expects it at the RE stage. But other than that, for research work also the
Department had asked for additional ` 500.00 cr. which the Department did not get.
3.3 On being enquired by the Committee as how the Department proposes to deal with this situation,
the Secretary, DSIR submitted before the Committee that this is of great concern in CSIR, especially
in the cutting edge National Labs. He further said that the CSIR is not a company and the Department
is contributing to the society by various means like education through fellowship and technologies
that make a difference to the lowest base of the pyramid. The return on investment may not be
impressive, but in terms of the social economic impact, it can be translated into money in actual
figures. The return is tremendous. If the Department is not supported financially, it will have
demoralizing influence on the scientists. The Department is still having a shortfall of about ` 350.00
cr. in core areas of Research & Development besides another shortfall of ` 150.00 cr. in salary and
pension. CSIR, thus, has been facing great challenges in pursuing the envisaged activities.
3.4 In view of the foregoing, CSIR sought intervention of the Committee for allocating an additional
budget of ` 500.00 cr. for the aforesaid activities during FY 2017-18. This will not only help CSIR
overcome the hardships but will also enable the Council to make continued contribution to the national
S&T programmes.
3.5 In view of the above submissions of the Department, the Committee feels that request
for the enhancement in the budgetary allocation to the tune of ````` 500.00 cr. for the financial
year 2017-18 is fully justified and the matter should be taken up by with the concerned
Ministry/Department vigorously. The Committee also observes that scientific institutions like
CSIR should not suffer due to lack of money especially in the cutting edge national labs
which are involved in various researches in the field of science.

8. COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC AND INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (CSIR)
8.1 The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research, constituted in 1942 is an autonomous body.
The detailed functions assigned to the Council are as follows:
(i) Promotion, guidance and coordination of scientific and industrial research in India,
including the institution and financing of specific researches;
(ii) Establishment or development and assistance to special institutions or departments of

11
existing institutions for scientific study of problems affecting particular industries and
trade;
(iii) Establishment and award of research studentships and fellowships;
(iv) Utilization of the results of the researches conducted under the auspices of the Council
towards the development of industries in the country and the payment of a share of
royalties arising out of the development of the results of researches to those who are
considered as having contributed towards the pursuits of such researches;
(v) Establishment, maintenance and management of laboratories, workshops, institutes and
organizations to further scientific and industrial research and to utilize and exploit for
purposes of experiment or otherwise any discovery or invention likely to be of use to
Indian industries;
(vi) Collection and dissemination of information in regard not only to research but also to
industrial matters generally;
(vii) Publication of scientific papers and journals;
(viii) To enter into arrangements with foreign scientific agencies and institutions for exchange
of scientists, study tours, training in specialized areas of science and technology,
conducting joint projects, providing technical assistance in the establishment of scientific
institutions and for other matters consistent with the aims and objectives of the Society;
(ix) To do all other such things as the Society may consider necessary, incidental or conducive
to the attainment of the above subjects, etc.
The CSIR has been striving to perform these functions in accordance with the priorities laid
down in Five Year Plans and perceived needs of the nation from time to time.
8.2 The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research is known for its cutting edge R&D knowledge
base in diverse S&T areas. Having pan-India presence, CSIR has a dynamic network of 38 National
Laboratories, 39 Outreach Centres, 3 Innovation Complexes and 5 units. CSIR’s R&D expertise and
experience is embodied in about 4000 active scientists supported by about 7000 scientific and technical
personnel.
8.3 CSIR covers a wide spectrum of science and technology from radio and space physics,
oceanography, earth sciences, geophysics, chemicals, drugs, genomics, biotechnology and
nanotechnology to mining, aeronautics, instrumentation, environmental engineering and information
technology. It provides significant technological intervention in many areas with regard to societal
efforts which include environment, health, drinking water, food, housing, energy, leather, farm and
non-farm sectors. CSIR is the Nation’s custodian for Measurement standards of Mass, Distance,
Time, Temperature, Current etc. CSIR has created and is the custodian of Traditional Knowledge
Digital Library (TKDL) which is a powerful weapon against unethical commercial exploitation of
Indian traditional knowledge. CSIR maintains Microbial Type Culture collection (MTCC) and Gene
Bank.
8.4 CSIR has been pursuing cutting edge science and advancing new knowledge frontiers. The
scientific staff of CSIR only constitutes about 3-4% of India’s scientific manpower but they contribute

12
to 9.61% of India’s scientific outputs. In 2013, 2014 and 2015 CSIR published 5086, 5824 and 5776
papers in SCI Journals with an average impact factor per paper of 2.86, 2.97 and 3.005 respectively.
During the year 2016, CSIR has published 5337 research papers in International SCI journals.
8.5 The Committee during its meeting on 15th February, 2017 was informed by the Department
that our scientific journals/papers in terms of scientific indices, its impact factor, quality, number of
citations our papers get, India is amongst top ten countries of the world. However, the Committee
had observed that some of the scientific journals/papers/ publications etc. of the research scholars
does not come out on time and also good work in respect of researches and inventions made very
often does not translate into sustainable technology for benefit of the citizens of the country.
8.6 The Committee notes and appreciates the efforts of CSIR in publishing large number
of research papers in International SCI journals every year. However, the Committee observes
that good work done by the CSIR in the form of research papers do not translate into
sustainable technologies for use of the masses. Hence, the Committee recommends that
Department should make all out efforts so that research and inventions may be translated
into sustainable technologies. The Committee further recommends that the scientific journals/
papers/ publications etc. should come out on time and with high standards.

10. EXAMINATION OF SOME OF THE CSIR-LABS /INSTITUTES/ORGANISATIONS:
The Committee has selected functioning of various scientific organisations/laboratories/

New Delhi to have the first hand information about the functioning of the Laboratory, scientific

NATIONAL PHYSICAL LABORATORY, NEW DELHI
10.1 The National Physical Laboratory was conceptualized in 1943 by the Governing Body of CSIR,
with a view to pave way for using science and technology as a means for industrial growth and
development, as well as to give fillip to the fledgling Indian industry. Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, the
then Prime Minister of India, laid the foundation stone for the laboratory on January 4, 1947 and it
was one of the first National Laboratory to be set-up under the CSIR. On January 21, 1950, Sardar
Vallabhbhai Patel, the then Deputy Prime Minister of India, inaugurated the NPL building. Over the
years, the Laboratory has more than realized its primary mandate as the keeper of Measurement
Standards for the nation while also substantially expanding its research activities to emerge as a
leading national institution for research in a whole gamut of areas in the Physical Science.
10.2 In the case of India, CSIR-NPL (internationally known as NPL-India) was designated the
National Metrology Institute (NMI) of the country through act of Parliament in 1957, with a
responsibility of realisation, establishment, maintenance and dissemination of seven base units and
derived units. Therefore, CSIR-NPL provides the metrological traceability at apex level and has
acted as growth engine of nation’s R&D and industries. Metrological traceability is property of a
measurement result whereby the result can be related to a reference through a documented unbroken
chain of calibrations, each contributing to the measurement uncertainty, and is very important for
international trade as it ensures the quality of the resultant products.
10.3 CSIR-National Physical Laboratory (NPL-India) is mandated to be India’s “National Measurement
Institute” (NMI) by act of Parliament and is the custodian of “National Standards” with a responsibility
of the dissemination of measurements to the needs of country.
10.4 Mission of the laboratory is as under:
(a) Developing India’s measurement standards that are internationally accepted and
disseminating the measurement capabilities to industry, government, strategic and
academia that underpin the India’s prosperity and quality of life.
(b) Conducting multidisciplinary R&D with a mission to establish the futuristic quantum
standards and upcoming technologies so that India remains on par with international
measurement laboratories.
(c) Developing sophisticated analytical equipments ( i.e. import substitutes) under “Make in
India” programme to cater the ever increasing demands of emerging India.
(d) Training of young scientists and industry personnel in the areas of measurements under
“Skill India” programme.

16
Vision of the laboratory is as under:
 To be “Giant in measurements” to support needs of the country
 To make NPL a “National hub” for the development of calibrated sophisticated instruments
 To make NPL a “Centre of Excellence” for skill development in the area of measurements
10.6 The Committee was informed that in order to achieve its mandated goals, the NPL has finalized
following five Mission Proposals (MP):
 Up-gradation and development of “National Apex Calibration Facilities”
 Setting up of “New Apex Calibration Facilities for Solar Cells, Biomedical- equipments
and Environmental-pollutants”
 Setting up of R&D Centre for “Quantum Standards”
 Materials & Devices for Strategic, Renewable-energy and Societal Applications
 Extending NPL facilities for Research and Industrial growth
10.7 The Committee was also briefed about the some major scientific contributions made by the
NPL in the past such as- Tractability of SI units to Indian R&D and Industries; Formula of Indelible
Ink for Election; Providing Indian Standard Time (1ST) to the country; Maitri - India’s permanent
research station in Antarctica; Advanced Carbon Product for strategic applications; and Providing
Indian Reference Materials.
The Committee during its visit to NPL also interacted with the Research Scholars / Scientists/

10.8 The Committee commends the role of NPL for its glorious achievements in the past in

would be able to excel in its field and also strive hard for its contribution towards nation

11. CSIR - NATIONAL AEROSPACE LABORATORIES (NAL), BENGALURU:
During its study visit to Bengaluru in August 2016, the Committee visited the CSIR-National
Aerospace Laboratories (NAL) and CSIR- Fourth Paradigm Institute (4PI) on the 31st August, 2016
and interacted with representatives of DSIR and these institutions.
11.1 At NAL, the Committee visited the exhibition at Autoclave facility, Wind Solar Hybrid Energy
Farm, Flight Simulator, Wind Thermal Facility and the Civil Aircraft Hanger and had a look at the
functioning and activities of these facilities. The Mandate of CSIR-NAL is to develop aerospace
technologies with strong science content, design and build small and medium-sized civil aircraft, and
support all national aerospace programmes. During the discussions, the Committee desired to know
the activities and achievements of NAL. Director, NAL, while giving a glimpse of the research,
scientific and technical work and the vision of NAL, informed that CSIR-NAL started in 1959 with
focus on development of technologies for Strategic Missions. The 1st blow down in the wind tunnel
facility was conducted in 1967. In early 70’s NAL developed the radomes for the meteorological

17
department and successfully completed the extension of Total life (TTL) of MiG 21s. In 80’s, NAL
successfully developed India’s 1st parallel computer. In 90’s NAL was the first laboratory to develop
the Composites technology and Autoclaves. During 1990 to 2000 NAL developed the 1st of its kind

12. CSIR-FOURTH PARADIGM INSTITUTE (4PI), BENGALURU
12.1 At CSIR-Fourth Paradigm Institute, the Committee visited the High Performance Computing
Facility. During the meeting, Director-4PI informed the Committee that CSIR Center for Mathematical
Modelling and Computer Simulation (C-MMACS) was set up in 1988 in NAL and was repositioned as
the Fourth Paradigm Institute (4PI) in 2013. The new Institute envisions creating expertise in
simulation, modelling and data science driven by high performance computing and data informatics.
It was informed that both these steps were forward looking since around 1988 the world’s fastest
supercomputer delivered only 333 MegaFlops whereas today the number stands at 93 PetaFlops.
Today modelling and simulation is taken for granted and is used across industries. On the other hand,
data science is gaining importance now and has already been commercially exploited by such industries
as Uber, Paytm etc. It was informed that data science has huge potential in scientific domain as well
and CSIR–4PI primarily aims to provide Knowledge products in the areas of Earth System and
Hazard with focus on Indian sub-continent and the data science will bring in new dimension in the
future and will synthesize the existing capabilities. Further elaborating on the Solid Earth Modelling
programme, it was informed that 4PI (C-MMACS) had many “firsts” to its credit. This group had,
for the first time in India, initiated work on Tomographic imaging of Earth, Kinematics and Crustal
Deformation of Indian Sub Continent and Seismic hazard map of India. Also, India’s first reference
GPS (Global Positioning System) station was set up in 1994 in Bangalore, which serves as a core
station for International terrestrial reference frame definition. Following these initiatives, C-MMACS

19
was instrumental in setting up National Network of GPS stations, precise quantification of continental
deformations, development of slip and rupture models associated with Bhuj and Sumatra–Andaman

in Kashmir Himalayas were established to investigate some puzzling features of the kinematics and
stress field in Kashmir Himalaya in collaboration with Kashmir University, Srinagar. These programmes

13. CSIR- CENTRAL GLASS & CERAMIC RESEARCH INSTITUTE (CGCRI), KOLKATA
During its study visit to Kolkata in October 2016, the Committee visited the CSIR- Central
Glass and Ceramic Research Institute (CGCRI) and CSIR- Indian Institute of Chemical Biology
(IICB) on 21st October, 2016 and interacted with representatives of DSIR and these institutions.
13.1 The Committee was briefed that need to establish a glass and silicate based materials laboratory
in British India was felt during Second World War due to emergent need of such materials for
purpose of war. The fledgling glass industry in particular was a hard hit and among many needs,
there were pleas by scientific community to open scientific research laboratories. In 1942, CSIR
was founded as Board of Scientific & Industrial Research (BSIR) in Kolkata, then Calcutta. At the
initiatives of renowned scientists, Prof. M. N. Saha, and Sir S. S. Bhatnagar, an exploratory report
was submitted to the BSIR for the possibility of organizing an Institute of glass research and the
Board appointed a Central Glass Research Institute Committee in March, 1942, as an advisory body.
After few important meetings, the body submitted its report to the BSIR for consideration in July,
1942. On July 12, 1943, on the recommendation of the BSIR, the Governing Body of the Board

20
decided that the proposed Institute for glass research be styled as the Central Glass and Silicate
Research Institute. The Institute ultimately took shape although in a limited ma nner in 1944 with
Dr. Atma Ram as officer-in-charge.
After Independence, the name of the Institute was changed to Central Glass and Ceramic
Research Institute and on August 26, 1950 the Institute was formally inaugurated.
13.2 Over last two decades, the R&D mandate of CGCRI has undergone major transformation in
order to adapt to the winds of globalisation. Today CGCRI is a premier organization pursuing R&D
in glass and various aspects of ceramics and ceramic based composite materials. In tune with the
national mission and CSIR’s theme-centric R&D paradigm, CGCRI is engaged in some of the high-
tech research-areas.
13.3 In addition to the two outreach centres, CGCRI comprises of 12 major R&D Divisions which
deal with various branches of glass and ceramics. These are namely: Advanced Clay and Traditional
Ceramics, Bioceramics and Coating, Ceramic Membrane, Glass Technology, Fibre Optics and
Photonics, Fuel Cell and Battery Nanostructured Materials, Non-oxide Ceramics Refractories Sensor
and Actuator and SoI-gel Processing.
13.4 Basically, CGCRl’s R&D programmes are focused towards: Technology Development, Training
and Entrepreneurship Development, Overseas/Sponsored/Contract Research Consultancy, Testing
and Materials Characterisation and Development and Supply of Special Materials. To meet the objective
of the country’s 12th Five Year Plan, CGCRI is engaged in six technology sectors of national priority
viz: Communication and Photonics, Energy and Environment, Health Care, Materials, Minerals and
Manufacturing, Rural Development and Water Technology.
13.5 During the meeting with the Committee, Director, CGCRI presented the overall activities of
the institute since its inception. This included an account of the scientific and technological activities,
patents and publications, technologies, the existing expertise of scientists, the different category of
employees, human resource, the students, project fellows, the national missions and technologies
for translation to industries with an aim to earn 30 to 40% revenue in coming years, existing number
of vacancies, plans for filling, training programs, technology dissemination and skill developments
initiated by the lab and other outreach centers in various areas and in various places, contributions
improving Industrial environment etc.
13.6 On being asked about the time required for transferring technologies from lab to products, the
Director, CGCRI informed the Committee that it takes about 20 years. The Committee also enquired
about the work /training carried out in the North-Eastern States of the country. On this, Director,
CGCRI replied that CGCRI has reached out to all the North -Eastern States of the country but the
numbers are less as this depends on the cooperation and encouragements from the local governments.
The Committee suggested disseminating the activities of the CGCRI lab to national level by initiating
discussion and interactions with state governments. The Committee enquired about earning revenue
while transferring technologies to many companies; the kind of agreements; subsidy given, if any;
and industry investments in the R&D. In response, Director, CGCRI answered that there is a unit
which looks at intellectual property rights, doing market survey and every time a technology is ready
an expression of interest is advertised. It was informed that some of the industries invest in the
R&D.

14. CSIR - INDIAN INSTITUTE OF CHEMICAL BIOLOGY (IICB), KOLKATA:

at present, the institute has six academic divisions: Cancer Biology & Inflammatory Disorder, Cell
Biology and Physiology, Organic and Medicinal Chemistry, Infectious Diseases and Immunology,

veil of mystery around the life. The spin-offs are bound to have a major impact on the health scenario

15. NATIONAL S&T HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMME
15.1 Human Resource Development is of paramount importance in the national building process
and creating a knowledge society. CSIR has focused in a significant manner on the development of
S&T Human Resource and has been rendering yeoman service by fostering, sustaining and helping in
upgradation of the stock of highly specialized scientists, engineers and technologists in diverse
disciplines of S&T, in the country. It awards fellowships, gives grants, and recognizes excellence
through various prizes and awards.
15.2 The main objectives of the National S&T Human Resources Development Programme are as
under:
 To promote and foster the upgradation of the stock of well qualified, highly specialized
scientists, engineers and technologists for R&D in all disciplines of Science & Technology
in the country
 To have an integrated approach to National Human Resource Development for Science,
Engineering & Technology by encouraging and promoting research in the Universities
and Institutes of higher learning
 To invest in basic and interdisciplinary research that is harbinger of the ‘high-tech’ and
technology of tomorrow.

amongst the government institutions as per the prestigious SCImago Institution Ranking. It has

in select technology domains. Commercialization of CSIR patents is 13.33% in comparison to ~3%

21. DUPLICATION IN RESEARCH WORK/ TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT
21.1 During its meeting held on 15th February, 2017, the Committee observes that similar kind of
research in various fields is going on in the Scientific Ministries/Departments of the country especially
in the Departments of Science & Technology, Scientific & Industrial Research, Biotechnology, and

33
Space and Ministry of Earth Sciences etc. For example, same type of devices like electronic machine
for checking blood pressure, blood sugar, water purifier, and milk adulteration is also developed by
the Department of Science and Technology (DST) and other Scientific Departments besides
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR).
21.2 The Committee further observes that research in same area could be done using different
methodology which could be later on compared to find out which one is better method and more
usability and financially viable for use of the masses. On responding to this, the Secretary of the
Department submitted that it looks like duplication because different Departments claim the credit
for it and present the results whereas they in fact collaborate. Moreover, especially, in case of
national labs, a specific project is presented with DST or DBT as well as CSIR, more often than not,

21.3 However, the Committee feels that this shows some sort of lack of co-ordination and
consultation between the various Scientific Ministries/ Departments of the country. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that a mechanism should be evolved for having a constant
and broad consultation/ co-ordination amongst the various scientific Ministries/ Departments
about the areas/fields of research so that time, energy, money, manpower and other resources
of the country may be utilized optimally.

inventions of public utilities, medicines, vaccines, varieties of rice, detection of milk adulteration

beneficial for the general public, researchers, academia, students, efforts of CSIR in skill development,

22.2 The Committee during its meeting held on 15th February, 2017 had also observed that
people of the country including elected representatives are not aware of the excellent work in
the field of Science being done by the Department or much about the Department itself which
may be beneficial for a very big segment of the society like farmers, fishermen, students,
research scholars etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should
prepare a comprehensive awareness programme with a calendar of events using social media
platforms, radio, television etc. meant for researchers, academia, farmers, industries, students
and general public but most importantly for all the elected representatives right from district
level i.e. Members of Zila Panchayats, Legislative Assemblies and Councils and Members of
Parliament. The Committee strongly feels that elected representatives can play an important
role in making their constituents aware of scientific development and ultimately developing
scientific temperament in the public at large.

The Committee also feels that to catch young students and nurture, groom and develop
them into budding scientists, it is imperative that a concerted and co-ordinated strategy is
made on a long- term basis. Since, CSIR has vast chain of scientific labs and the biggest
institution as employer of scientists; it has to actively play a major role in this direction. Just
by awarding some fellowships/ Scholarships, this mammoth task is not going to be accomplished.
Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Department must come out some concrete
proposals to trap, harness and retain human resources in the field of science. (Para 15.9)
FILING AND GRANT OF PATENTS
The Committee appreciates the efforts of CSIR in obtaining patents in India and abroad.
However, the Committee feels that ratio in respect of Patents filed and Patents granted in India
and abroad is not encouraging. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Department should
have constant vigil on this front and also the matter may be taken up vigorously with National
Biodiversity Authority (NBA) for clearance of around 150 patents, in order to file the same with
the Indian Patent Office in the field of Biological Sciences, at the ea rliest. (Para 16.4)
WORLD RANKING OF CSIR
The Committee notes with satisfaction that CSIR has improved its world ranking among
Government institutions as well as its overall global Ranking. However, the Committee
observes that CSIR is still far behind amongst the globally benchmarked scientific organisations
in the world. The Committee, therefore, recommends that in order to place India in the list
of the top countires in the scientific world , CSIR should aim to become amongst at least first
10 global organisations in its field and it should strive hard to achieve that rank ing.(Para 17.3)
PROJECTS/ SCHEMES IN NORTH – EASTERN STATES
The Committee notes the initiatives taken by the Department in the form of various
projects/ schemes being run in the North-Eastern States of the country which will bring the
qualitative changes in the lives of the people of that area and also generate employment
opportunities. However, the Committee feels that lot more is needed to be done in order to
augment the incomes and improve the quality of lives of millions of people geographically
spread across the North-Eastern States of the country. (Para 18.6)
SKILL DEVELOPMENT
The Commi ttee appreciates the efforts of the Department in this matter and hopes that it
will yield desired results and will go a long way in respect of social upliftment of down-trodden
persons of the society. However, the Committee feels that merely running new skill programs
in the areas of Leather Processing Technology, Industrial Maintenance Engineering,

39
Mechatronics, Instrumentation, Battery maintenance, Internet of Things, Advance
Manufacturing Technology, etc. is not enough unless those skilled persons are employed or
integrated in the respective industries . Therefore, the Committee recommends that Department
should have linkages with various industries as well Ministries/ Departments so that these
skilled persons could get suitable employment and sustain their livel ihoods. (Para 19.4)
CSIR’S ROYALTY AND EARNINGS OF DEPARTMENT BY TECHNOLOGY TRANSFER
The Committee observes that income of the Department from royalty component is
very low as compared to the huge investment of the Government on account of research/
innovations/ R&D etc. vis-à-vis  profit earned by the private companies/industries by making
commercial use of technologies developed by the Department. In view of this, the Committee
recommends that MoU should be signed with the companies/industries for fixing royalty
component while making technology transfer/inventions for allowing its product for commercial
utilization so that Department could be financially self reliant in every aspect and invest in
R&D. (Para 20.4)
The Committee, therefore, recommends that investment in R&D must be increased so
that research work may be taken up at large scale and more and more representatives of
industries/companies should be motivated for making investment in R&D of the Scientific
Ministries/Departments of the country. (Para 20.6)
The Committee further is of the opinion that instead of giving the technologies to private
companies/ industries in the first instances, option for exploring transfer of technologies to
Public Sector companies may be explored which could be beneficial for both i.e.  Department
as well as Public Sector companies. In order to achieve this goal, the Committee recommends
that more tie-ups between the Department and Public Sector companies/ institutions should
be done. (Para 20.7)
DUPLICATION IN RESEARCH WORK/ TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT
However, the Committee feels that this shows some sort of lack of co-ordination and
consultation between the various Scientific Ministries/Departments of the country. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that a mechanism should be evolved for having a constant
and broad consultation/ co-ordination amongst the various scientific Ministries/ Departments
about the areas/fields of research so that time, energy, money, manpower and other resources
of the country may be utilized optimally. (Para 21.3)
AWARENESS AND OUTREACH PROGRAMME OF THE DEPARTMENT
The Committee during its meeting held on 15th February, 2017 had also observed that
people of the country including elected representatives are not aware of the excellent work in
the field of Science being done by the Department or much about the Department itself which
may be beneficial for a very big segment of the society like farmers, fishermen, students,
research scholars etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department should
prepare a comprehensive awareness programme with a calendar of events using social media
platforms, radio, television etc. meant for researchers, adacemia, farmers, industries, students

40
and general public but most importantly for all the elected representatives right from district
level i.e. Members of Zila Panchayats, Legislative Assemblies and Councils and Members of
Parliament. The Committee strongly feels that elected representatives can play an important
role in making their constituents aware of scientific development and ultimately developing
scientific temperament in the public at large. (Para 22.2)

REPORT
INTRODUCTION
In terms of Rule 270 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Rajya Sabha,
examination of budgetary proposals is one of the primary mandates of the Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committees. In this context, the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests considered the Demands for Grants of
the Ministries/Departments within its purview during the third week of February, 2017. This Report of
the Committee deals with the examination of the Demands for Grants for the year 2017-18 (Demand
No.91) of the Department of Space. The Committee considered the Demands for Grants (2017-18) of
the Department of Space in its meeting held on 16th February, 2017.
2. ORGANISATION
2.1 Space activities in our country were initiated with the setting up of Indian National Committee
for Space Research (INCOSPAR) in 1962. Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) was established
in August 1969. The Government of India has set up the Space Commission and the Department of
Space (DOS) in 1972. The DOS is responsible for implementing the policies framed by the Space
Commission. These are carried out through the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the
Grant-in-aid institutions viz., Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), National Atmospheric Research
Laboratory (NARL), North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC), Semi-Conductor Laboratory
(SCL) and Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST).
2.2 The Secretariat of the Department of Space and the Headquarters of ISRO are located in Bengaluru.
The Programme Offices at ISRO Headquarters co-ordinate the overall programmes like satellite
communication, satellite navigation, earth observation, launch vehicle, space science, atmospheric
science, space industry development, disaster management support, international co-operation,
publications and public relations, budget and economic analysis and human resources development.
2.3 The m ajor Centres, Units and establishments of DOS/ISRO, responsible for carrying out
research and development activities as well as for undertaking various projects and programmes,
are given below:
(a) Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC), Thiruvananthapuram, provides the technology
base for the country’s indigenous launch vehicle (rocket) development;
(b) Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC), with its facilities located at Bengaluru and
Thiruvananthapuram is responsible for development of liquid propulsion and cryogenic
propulsion systems for satellite and launch vehicles;
(c) ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC), erstwhile LPSC, Mahendragiri has the responsibility
for assembly, integration and testing of storable and cryogenic liquid rocket engines and
stages, spacecraft thrusters testing in sea level and high altitude conditions, storage of
liquid and cryogenic propellants and production of liquid hydrogen etc.
(d) Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh, is the spaceport
of India providing launch base to indigenously built launch vehicles. Also, it provides the
facilities for processing of solid rocket motors;

2
(e) ISRO Satellite Centre (ISAC), Bengaluru, is entrusted with the prime responsibility for
development of satellites;
(f) The Laboratory for Electro-Optics Systems (LEOS), Bengaluru has the responsibility for
development and productionisation of electro-optical sensors for satellites;
(g) Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad, carries out research and development in
space applications as well as development of application payloads;
(h) Development and Educational Communication Unit (DECU), Ahmedabad, is involved in
the conception, definition, planning and socio/techno-economic evaluation of development
communication programmes;
(i) National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC), Hyderabad is responsible for satellite data
acquisition and processing, data dissemination, aerial remote sensing and decision support
for disaster management.
(j) Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS), Dehradun is a premier training and educational
institute set up for developing trained professionals in the field of Remote Sensing, Geo-
informatics and GPS Technology for Natural Resources, Environmental and Disaster
Management.
(k) ISRO Telemetry, Tracking & Command Network (ISTRAC), with its ground stations at
Bengaluru, Sriharikota, Lucknow, Bearslake, Russia, Biak (Indonesia), Brunei, Mauritius
etc. provides the telemetry, tracking and command support and spacecraft mission
management for the Indian remote sensing satellite missions, space science missions and
satellite launch vehicle programmes;
(l) Master Control Facility (MCF) with its main facility at Hassan in Karnataka and backup
facility at Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh has the responsibility for control and operation of
INSAT/GSAT/METSAT satellites;
(m) ISRO Inertial Systems Unit (IISU), Thiruvananthapuram, carries out research and
development in the area of inertial systems for satellites and launch vehicles.
2.4 Also, a National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS), with the Department of
Space (DOS) as the nodal agency, has been established to ensure optimal utilisation of natural resources
using remote sensing data in conjunction with conventional techniques. Under NNRMS, five Regional
Remote Sensing Service Centres (RRSSCs) at Bengaluru, Dehradun, Jodhpur, Kolkata and Nagpur
have been set up for execution of remote sensing application programmes in the respective regions.
Organisations receiving Grants-in-aid:
(a) Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad, an autonomous institution supported
mainly by the Department of Space, carries out research in space sciences.
(b) The National Atmospheric Research Laboratory (NARL) set up at Gadanki near Tirupati,
conducts atmospheric research.
(c) The North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC) established as an autonomous

3
body under the Department of Space provides space technology inputs for developmental
activities in the North-Eastern Region.
(d) The Semi-conductor Laboratory (SCL) located at Chandigarh is a research and development
society and is entrusted with the design and development of Very Large Scale Integrated
Circuit (VLSI) devices and development of micro-electronic systems to meet the strategic
needs of the country.
(e) The Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST) is an autonomous body
under the Department with the objective of creating quality human resources tuned to suit
the requirements of state-of-art space research programme. The Institute offers graduate,
post-graduate and doctoral programmes in the area of space science, technology and
applications. The annual intake of the Institute is about 150-200 students.
2.5 Apart from this, RESPOND programme of ISRO supports sponsored research activity in space
science, space applications and space technology in various national academic/research institutions
and Space Technology Cells in premier technological institutes of the country through grants-in-aid.
Antrix Corporation Limited
2.6 Antrix Corporation Limited (ACL), Bengaluru is a wholly owned Government of India Company
under the administrative control of the Department of Space. Antrix Corporation Limited was incorporated
as a private limited company owned by Government of India in September 1992 as a marketing arm of
ISRO for promotion and commercial exploitation of space products, technical consultancy services
and transfer of technologies developed by ISRO. Another major objective is to facilitate development of
space related industrial capabilities in India. As the commercial and marketing arm of ISRO, Antrix is
engaged in providing space products and services to international customers worldwide. With fully
equipped state-of-the-art facilities, Antrix provides end-to-end solution for many of the space products,
ranging from supply of hardware and software including simple subsystems to a complex spacecraft,
for varied applications covering communications, earth observation and scientific missions; space related
services including remote sensing data service, Transponder lease service; Launch services through
the operational launch vehicles (PSLV and GSLV); Mission support services; and a host of consultancy
and training services.

YEAR PLAN PERIOD
