INTRODUCTION
The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change is the nodal agency in the administrative
structure of the Central Government for planning, promoting, co-ordinating and overseeing environmental,
ecological, forestry and wildlife policies and programmes. Its main activities include conservation and
survey of natural resources including flora, fauna, forests, wildlife, aquatic bodies and water resources
and eco-systems, prevention and control of pollution and management of hazardous substances, protection
of the environment and forests, including their biodiversity, mitigation and adaptation to climate change
through measures that include afforestation, regeneration of degraded areas, and adoption of cleaner
technologies, and promoting sustainable development and better environmental governance while protecting
human, plants and animals life, health and welfare.
1.2 The main tools used to discharge its mandate include, inter alia,  conducting surveys; collecting,
compiling and disseminating data and information; undertaking scientific research, extension services and
analyses; carrying out impact assessment of developmental projects and programmes; regulating use of
natural resources; undertaking regeneration programmes; extending technical, scientific, financial and
administrative support to organisations and institutions in the subject fields; imparting education, training,
building capacity and generating awareness among stakeholders and the public at large; and promoting
international co-operation through bilateral, regional and multilateral initiatives in environment and ecology.
1.3. The institutional set up of the Ministry includes a number of Directorates and Divisions assembled
around the main thematic sectors of environment and ecology, national river conservation, forestry and
wildlife, afforestation and eco-development, and animal welfare. The Ministry has ten Regional Offices;
twelve Attached/Subordinate Offices (e.g. Botanical, Zoological and Forest Survey of India, and Directorate
of Forestry Education); Boards and Authorities (e.g. Central Pollution Control Board, National Biodiversity
Authority, National Tiger Conservation Authority, Central Zoo Authority and Animal Welfare Board of
India); Autonomous Institutions ( e.g. Indian Council for Forestry Research and Education and Wildlife
Institute of India); and one Public Sector Undertaking, namely, the Andaman & Nicobar Islands Forest
Plantation Development Corporation Ltd. at Port Blair. Provision has been made in the Demands for

4.2 The Committee desired to know the reasons for lower expenditure in 2016-17 as well as the whole
12th Five year Plan period. The Ministry informed the Committee that the lower utilistion in 2016-17 was
mainly on account of general administrative and procedural reasons, like delays in receipt of proposals,
lack of adequate proposals, non/late submission of Utilisation Certificates, revalidation of unspent balances,
completion of works, etc. In many schemes, implementing agencies are State Governments/Forest
Departments, whose performance depends on timely release of matching grants. Time lag in release of
funds by the Ministry and actual availability of funds to such implementing agencies also impacts on the
performance of these schemes. It was also informed that regular meetings are held with the Divisional
Heads in-charge of the Programmes/Schemes to expedite utilization levels. Instructions have been issued
to the Programme Divisions/autonomous bodies/ attached offices from time-to-time to improve the pace
of utilization.
4.3 The Committee notes the reasons for shortfall in utilisation of funds furnished by Ministry
of Environment, Forest & Climate Change. The Committee had come across identical reasons
for underutilization while examining the Demands for Grants 2016-17 of Ministry of Environment,
Forest & Climate Change and had recommended the Ministry to take a review of its financial
performance. In this context, the Committee would like to reiterate the recommendation made
in its 283rd Report on Demands for Grants (2016-17) of Ministry of Environment, Forest &
Climate Change which is as under:-
"Most of the reasons cited by the Ministry for under-utilisation of funds are administrative and
procedural which could have been avoided. This also shows lack of planning and foresightedness
on part of the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should undertake
a review of its financial performance during the last few years and try to identify the bottlenecks
responsible for not being able to optimally utilise the funds at its disposal so as to improve its
performance on this front in the future".

10. ZOOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
10.1 The Committee was informed that Zoological Survey of India (ZSI) was established in 1916
primarily to explore and inventorise faunal resources (diversity) and to collect and document base line
data on taxonomy, distribution, bio-ecology, etc. of all available animal groups. Since then, it has grown
from a small unit at the Indian Museum (Kolkata) to a premier National Institution, with Headquarters
at Kolkata, and 16 Regional Centres. ZSI serves the nation by providing scientific basis for conservation
and sustainable utilisation of faunal diversity through survey, inventory, monitoring documentation, capacity
building, and taxonomic research and creating environmental awareness.
10.2 The Committee was informed that the Physical achievements of ZSI since reorganisation till now
are broadly as follows:
(i) ZSI surveyed and documented 49 PAs.
(ii) Scientists of ZSI discovered 4,346 new species, more than 1,000 new records.
(iii) ZSI maintains and displays 3,833 exhibits in 6 Galleries in the Indian Museum (Mammal; Bird;
Ecology; Reptilia & Amphibia; Fish; and Insect).
(iv) Status survey carried out of Black-buck, Mouse Deer, Swamp Deer, Four Horned Antelope,
Sasu, Goral, Coral reefs, Coral-associated Organisms, Rock Toad, Hill Myna, Chinkara, Desert
Cat, Non-Human Primates, Serow, Indian Golden Gecko and Varanus species.
(v) Taxonomic studies carried out on Protozoa, Helminthes, Mollusca, Annelida, Cnidaria, Porifera
(Sponges), Echinodermata, Insecta, Arachnida, Pisces (Fishes), Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves (Birds)
and Mammals, along with Tricho-taxonomic studies on Mammals and molecular studies on
Freshwater turtles.
(vi) Published faunal documents under the State Fauna Series (Andaman & Nicobar-1; Andhra
Pradesh-8; Arunachal Pradesh-2; Bihar, including Jharkhand-1; Delhi-1; Goa-1; Gujarat-2;
Karnataka-1; Lakshadweep-1; Madhya Pradesh, including Chhattisgarh-3; Manipur-3; Meghalaya-
10; Mizoram-2; Nagaland-1; Odisha-4; Sikkim-5; Tamil Nadu-2; Tripura-4; Uttarakhand-3; and

(a) Taxonomy, as the mother of all science, was getting poorer day by day and taxonomists have
become endangered. They matured through experience. Revenue generation should not be the
primary aim particularly with respect to taxonomy, which has been providing the broad
knowledge base, about the biological wealth and therefore, scientific staff requirement for the
Zoological Survey of India is of prime importance.
(b) Due importance was not given to ZSI, although they were looking after very important work
like identification of seized materials to the enforcement agencies. Insufficient number of
serving scientific officials (Gr. A and B) and staff (Gr. C) has been an issue in ZSI for the
past 20 years. Besides the filling up of vacancies, infrastructure like wildlife forensic laboratories
in 4 to 5 centres of ZSI could be facilitated.
(c) Non availability of forest entry permissions, which often remained as an impediment for the
department in delivering their duties and responsibilities and therefore, importance of
collaborations to be established between ZSI, BSI and forest departments. At least one taxonomist
(Biologist) in all the Protected Areas as well as in the forest department must be appointed
which could serve to enhance the detailed scientific aspects of the flora and fauna, thereby
adding to their income through tourism. This initiative would in turn generate employment for
taxonomists and indirectly, the science would remain nurtured.
(d) Like through IFS, the terrestrial forests were studied and protected, and therefore, there is a
need for setting up a separate wing to study and conserve the bio resources of the marine
realm/oceans through the marine biologists.
(e) The budget for ZSI has to be increased substantially, taking into consideration the quantum
of duties and quality of research work the organisation is performing including training
programmes and workshops proposed.
(f) The curriculum of probationary civil servants, to look upon forests as a pool to tap resources
and the values of conservation was yet to be highlighted with due seriousness and ZSI may

15
be asked to offer short term training to IAS/IFS on faunal diversity. Therefore, training to Civil
Servants (all cadres) on Environment related aspects may be taken up in ZSI.
(g) Foreign visits/training to scientists of world class stature in the organisations was yet to
materialise. Under the head of Capacity building, bilateral exchange programs of scientists
could be organised with renowned World class institutions like British Museum, and approved
by MoEFCC.
(h) Development of DNA Banks and reference gene libraries for faunal elements are extremely
important requirements which will serve as National Facility for research, management and
conservation of faunal elements of India. This national facility will also generate revenue by
exchanging the genetic material through research collaborations within and between the countries
through government to government interactions and policy decisions. The genetic information
developed in this national facility will be used in agricultural research like pest control, biomedical
research for diseases resistant, ecological research, conservation biology, etc.
(i) ZSI may start two new Centres of Zoological Survey of India in Sikkim and Gujarat as a mark
towards service for 100 years of the organisation to the country.
(j) Atoll systems also hold tremendous potential for conducting globally significant research on
weather patterns, climate change, and understanding biogeochemical, geological, physical
dynamics of the Oceans. Therefore, ZSI may propose an Atoll Research Centre at Lakshadweep.
(k) Tunnel Aquarium may be set up at ZSI, Digha jointly with the help of Government of West
Bengal as announced by the then Hon'ble Minister of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
during his visit to ZSI on the occasion of centenary celebrations.
(l) In order to augment the ever increasing demand for space, it was informed to the Committee
that ZSI has approached the West Bengal Government with a request to provide it with a
parcel of land within Kolkata city limits so that ever increasing needs for space to accommodate
our precious collection holdings of faunal repository shall be met with effectively. Therefore,
ZSI may send proposal to Government of India for funding and accordingly, construct new
office-cum-museum-cum-residential buildings comprising of administrative block, conference
room, State-of-art Museum on faunal biodiversity, aquarium, molecular laboratory, faunal
genebank, National repository on Indian Fauna, training centre, visiting scientist hostel beside
residential complex.
(m) Services rendered by CPWD are required to be improved for ZSI.
10.5 The Committee recommends that Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
should look into all the above issues that emerged during the meeting with the representatives
of ZSI and take necessary action thereon, as the Committee feels that all these issues merit full
consideration.
10.6 During the visit, the Committee observed that the building of ZSI was in a dilapidated condition.
Further, due to the limited resources, the authorities are unable to keep valuable specimens properly and

16
they have been kept in a very shabby manner. Further, they were not able to keep the boxes/rooms where
the specimens were kept temperature controlled, which is extremely essential for them.
10.7 The Committee is of the view that certain specimens conserved in ZSI are irreplaceable and
some of them have even become extinct in our country. The specimens are our national assets
and they should be conserved befittingly. It is sad and alarming to note that due to resource
constraints, the concerned authorities are unable to preserve the specimen with modern
technologies. The Committee recommends that the entire building of ZSI should be upgraded and
modernised in a time bound manner, on a top priority basis. The rooms/boxes where the specimens
are kept should be temperature controlled. The modernization of the building would also enable
the specimens to be displayed in a way so that visitors could have a good look at them. ZSI is
one the country's most valuable resource centers and, therefore, the building and the conservation
areas should be modernised in a manner reflecting their importance and their place in Indian
history. The Committee also recommends that adequate budgetary allocation should be made for
the renovation and modernisation of the building and the specimen conserving/preserving areas.
11. BOTANICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
11.1 The Botanical Survey of India (BSI) is the apex research organisation under the Ministry of
Environment, Forest and Climate Change for carrying out taxonomic and floristic studies of wild plant
resources of the country through survey, documentation and conservation. It was established on 13th
February, 1890 with the basic objective to explore the plant resources of the country and to identify the
plants species with economic virtues. The Physical achievements of the Institution since its reorganisation
in 1954 are broadly as follows:
(i) Survey and exploration of about 70 per cent of India's geographical areas completed for
vascular plants, which resulted in a Repository of 4 million National Reference collections of
plant specimens.
(ii) New family of lowering plants and 34 new genera have been described, 961 species and
numerous infra-specific-taxa discovered as new to science.
(iii) Inventory of about 1,700 Rare, Endangered and Threatened (RET) species undertaken.
(iv) Live collection of over 1.5 lakh plants in Indian Botanic Garden, Botanic Garden of Indian
Republic and associated botanic gardens and National Orchidaria of regional Offices.
(v) Flowering plants of 7 Biosphere Reserves, 39 National Parks, 8 Wildlife Sanctuary and 28
Tiger Reserves documented.
(vi) Hepaticae and anthocerotae (Bryophytes) of Great Himalayan National park (Himachal Pradesh)
and Mehao Wildlife Sanctuary (Arunachal Pradesh) documented.
(vii) Lichens of Sunderbans Biosphere Reserve (West Bengal) documented
(viii) Traditional Knowledge on plants associated with tribes belonging to 41 districts of Bihar
Jharkhand, Karnataka, Odisha and Rajasthan and over 114 tribes belonging to Andaman and

17
Nicobar Islands, Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Jammu and Kashmir, Madhya
Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and West
Bengal documented. Seventeen books on Ethno-botany published by BSI Scientists.
(ix) EIA studies on impact of over 100 developmental projects on flora completed.
(x) Over 150 research scholars trained in different aspects of plant systematic, leading to award
of Doctorate degree by various Indian Universities.
(xi) Over 3 million herbarium specimens of India nearly 2 lakhs from different adjoining countries
and rest of the world are housed in herbaria of BSI. These include 16,000 type specimens
(original material based on which species new to science is described).
(xii) Over 18,000 exhibits, tannins, dies, oils, fibers, timbers, medicinal, beverages, vegetables, food
and tribal artifacts in Kolkata and all Circle Offices.
(xiii) Nine volumes of National Flora, 24 Fascicles of Flora of India; 43 volumes of State Flora: 35
volumes of District Flora; 4 volumes of Red Data Book of Indian Plants and Red List species
of India and 145 titles dealing with various thematic topics related to India flora published.
(xiv) 23 volumes of 'Records of the Botanical Survey of India; 54 volumes of 'Bulletin of the
Botanical Survey of India; 20 volumes of 'V anaspati V ani' and 17 volumes of 'ENVIS Newsletters'
already published.
(xv) Monitored critically endangered species/population, like Cycas Beddomei (Deccan Plateau);
Trachycerpus Takii (West Bengal), Gymnociadus Assamicus and G. Burmanicus (NL).

15. CHIRU GOAT (TIBETAN ANTELOPE)
15.1 During the meeting of the Committee held on 14th February 2017, the Committee, while discussing
Wildlife Conservation, observed that Chiru Goats were being used by certain communities in Jammu and
Kashmir for extracting wool and making shahtoosh shawls. The Committee desired to know about
wildlife status of the chiru goats. In response, the Committee was informed by the Ministry of Environment,
Forest and Climate Change that Tibetan antelope (Panthelop hodgsoni)  from which the shahtoosh is
derived is included under Schedule-I of Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. This species is highly endangered
and any commercial trade is strictly prohibited. There are only few animals left in the wild and as it is
critically endangered, the species is listed in Schedule-I of the Act, thereby according it highest degree
of protection. Hunting of the species and trade of its parts and products, including shawls made of Chiru
wool are prohibited under the Act. Any contravention of the provision of the Act, attracts stringent
penalties. As Chiru cannot be used for extraction of wool for shahtoosh wool as per the prevalent Act,
alternate livelihood for the affected communities needs to be taken up by the State Government. The
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change would extend support for alternative livelihood for
the affected communities.
15.2 The Committee feels that Jammu and Kashmir has been the conflict region for long and
many women there are unable to leave their homes and go out for livelihood. The shawl walas
who live there have been accused of killing the chiru goat in order to procure the wool for
making a shahtoosh shawl. However, the shawl makers say that they do not kill the goats
because if they kill a goat for every shawl, where will the shawls be produced from. The
Committee understands that China and Mongolia are breeding the chiru goats and Mongolia is

23
known for its finest wool. The Committee feels that livelihood opportunities are very low for the
people of Jammu and Kashmir because of the extreme climatic conditions there and shawl
making contributes a lot towards sustainable livelihoods of these people. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should conserve and
breed the chiru goat and vast tract of land should be utilised for conserving the chiru goats.
These goats can then be given to the shawl makers for collecting hair. This would not only
increase the number of these goats but would also add to the sustainable livelihood opportunities
of the people of Jammu and Kashmir , who are a lot dependant on the handicraft of embroidered
shawls.
16. THE CAMPA FUNDS
16.1 During the meeting of the Committee held on 14th February 2017, the Secretary of the Ministry,
in his presentation, informed the Committee that the Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act 2016 was
passed on the 3rd August 2016. The Act provides for the establishment of funds under the public
accounts of India and the public accounts of each State and crediting thereto the monies received from
the user agencies. The money is to be utilized for undertaking artificial regeneration (plantations), assisted
natural regeneration, protection of forests, forest related infrastructure development, Green India
Programme, wildlife protection and other related activities. In response to a query whether plantations
under CAMPA can be used for commercial viability, the representative of the Ministry informed the
Committee as under:
"No, Madam. It is not like that. There are two parts of CAMP A funds. One is about compensatory
afforestation. In that, either an area equal to the piece of land from where trees were removed for
non-forestry purpose, or, in some cases, double the degraded forest land has to be planted. It is not
necessary that these plantations will be of single species. It is not like that. It is not meant for
commercial purpose. This is basically compensation for the loss of the forest which had been
diverted for non-forestry purpose. The sentence here means compensatory afforestation. Also, we are
doing artificial regeneration as a part of the NPV (Net Present Value) funds. It is for the loss of
ecosystem services. It is not commercial plantation."
16.2 The Committee expressed apprehension that some reports suggested that Ministry of Road Transport
and Highways intended to do tree plantations along the National Highways using CAMPA funds. It was
also brought out that during its study visit to some States, the Committee was informed that CAMPA
funds were being used for many activities which otherwise do not come under the ambit of CAMPA or
had no relation whatsoever with the afforestation activities. In response, the Ministry informed the
Committee that the CAMPA funds are utilized as per the Guidelines of the Adhoc CAMPA which was
constituted by the Hon'ble Supreme Court. CAMPA has come into being with effect from 3rd August,
2016 and the Ministry is now in the process of framing rules in consultation with the States and
concerned stake holders so as to provide uniformity in the utilization of compensatory levies collected
as yet.
16.3 The Committee notes that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change is in
the process of framing rules in consultation with the State Governments and concerned stake

24
holders for the utilisation of the CAMPA Funds. The Committee is perturbed to note the reports
emanating from various quarters that the CAMPA funds are being utilized for purposes other
than they are intended for. The Committee recommends that while framing the rules, the
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change must ensure that the rules do not give any
scope for mis-utilisation or embezzlement of the funds by the States or any other stake holders.
The Ministry must also devise a stringent monitoring mechanism to ensure that the CAMPA
funds are utilized for the intended purposes only.

18. CENTRE OF EXCELLENCE - CENTRE FOR ECOLOGICAL SCIENCES, (INDIAN INSTITUTE
OF SCIENCE), BENGALURU.
18.1 The Scheme Centre of Excellence was initiated in the Year 1983. The objective of the Scheme is
to provide 'selective support' to Universities, reputed institutions including NGOs, professional organisations
and other scientific and technical institutions to enable them to develop into advanced Centres at the
national level in that particular subject area. The broad objectives of the scheme are as under:
• To enhance and strengthen the country's human, scientific technological, organizational,
institutional and resource capabilities with a view to achieving economic development without
damaging the environment.
• To encourage and support universities/institutions, NGOs to undertake activities to develop or
strengthen the capacities and capabilities of the identified units so that they may contribute to
the process of the sustainable development.
• To enhance and upgrade existing skills, knowledge and technical know-how of the universities/
research institutions/NGOs so that may be able to integrate environment and development.
• To enhance the efficiency of existing universities, institutions and NGOs for devising national
sustainable development strategies in partnership with the Ministry of Environment, Forests
and Climate Change.
• To create awareness among various sections of the population of the country regarding
environmental issues with a view to encourage and enhancing public participation in the
programmes and activities of the MoEF&CC.
18.2 At present, there are eight Centres of Excellence which are operational under different themes. CES,
IISc, Bengaluru is one of them. The CES, IISc, functions under the Indian Institute of Science and
carries out projects agreed to and approved by the Research Advisory and Monitoring Committee
(RAMC) constituted by MoEF&CC for which the financial assistance is provided by the MoEF&CC. The
CES, IISc undertakes research with practical applications in frontline areas of ecology/environment of
the Western Ghats under the following themes:
(a) Community, forest and wildlife ecology
(b) Animal Behaviour and Evolution
(c) Human and Landscape Ecology
(d) Climate Change and its Impact
(e) Conservation Outreach, Training and Education
18.3 CES is engaged in high quality original research on the biodiversity of the Western Ghats which is
one of the global hotspots of biodiversity. This research ranges from microfauna such as ants and

26
termites to megafauna such as elephants, as well as the floristics and ecology of tropical forests. Unique
research being conducted in CES involves such subjects as (1) acoustic sampling of the biodiversity of
tropical forests, (2) reconstruction of the palaeoclimate of the southern Western Ghats with bearing on
present scenarios of climate change, (3) investigating the impact of atmospheric pollution such as
tropospheric ozone on the half-life of chemical signals emitted by plants to attract their pollinating insects,
and (4) long-term research on tropical forest dynamics and carbon sequestration. Research in CES has
not solely been concentrated on the terrestrial ecology of the Western Ghats but has also been focused
on freshwater ecosystems including freshwater fish and molluscs. Over the years, since its inception,
this research has resulted in 1024 research papers, 25 books, and 122 technical reports. The research
papers of CES have been published in international and national scientific journals of high repute. In
recognition of their outstanding caliber, CES faculty have also been elected to national and international
Science Academies such as the National Academy of Sciences (USA), The World Academy of Sciences,
Indian Academy of Sciences and the Indian National Science Academy. Members of the CES faculty have
also received prestigious awards such as the Order of the Golden Ark and the International Cosmos Prize
for their conservation-related research.
18.4 The scientific output/information/data collected by the Centre of Ecological Sciences are used by
the various departments/research institutions of the country. The information is disseminated through
publishing technical research papers in the national and international journals, organizing conference/
seminar/symposia, publishing of books and putting the achievements on the website on CES/IISc. The
information is also shared with ENVIS for use by the various departments of the Ministry.

19. INTEGRATED DEVELOPMENT OF WILDLIFE HABITATS
19.1 The Committee was informed that this Centrally sponsored Scheme has the following components:-
(a) Project Tiger
19.2 India launched the holistic "Project Tiger" in 1973 to conserve our critically endangered national
animal - the tiger. Based on the recommendations of the Tiger Task Force, the Wildlife (Protection) Act,
1972 was amended in 2006 for creating the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) to give
statutory support for strengthening tiger conservation. The coverage of "Project Tiger" has increased
from 9 reserves since inception to 48 tiger reserves spread out in 18 States of the country in 2015.
Though the focus is on the flagship / umbrella species 'tiger' the project strives to maintain the stability
of ecosystem by fostering other tropic levels in the food chain thereby ensuring healthy forests, clean
air, clean water and a clean environment. NTCA retains oversight through advisories / normative guidelines,
based on appraisal of tiger status, ongoing conservation initiatives and recommendations of specially
constituted Committees. All India Tiger Estimation, 2014 results shows that India now has 2226 tigers
which are 30% increase over the last count and is 70% of the total global tiger population.
(b) Project Elephant
19.3 Project Elephant was launched in 1991-92 as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme with following
objectives:
(i) To protect elephants, their habitat and corridors;
(ii) To address issues of man-animal conflict; and
(iii) Welfare of domesticated elephant.
19.4 The Committee was informed that financial and technical assistance is being provided to major
elephant bearing States in the country. Under the scheme, 100% financial assistance is provided to the
concerned State Government for undertaking various activities for scientific management of elephant

29
habitats. Presently, the project is being implemented in 22 States / UTs. There are 29 notified and 3
proposed Elephant Reserves in the country, which are still to be notified by the concerned State
Governments, covering approximately 65,000 sq. km. area.
19.5 The Committee noted that the allocation for Project Tiger and Project Elephant had been reduced
at RE stage in 2016-17 and desired to know the reasons therefor. The Committee also enquired as to
whether the Ministry was able to achieve its targets, physical as well as financial, in respect of the above
projects during the year?
19.6 As regards Project Tiger, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change submitted as
under:
(i) North Eastern tiger range States have not submitted the proposal as per tentative allocation and
for Village relocation due to which reduction has been proposed. As a result allocation of
` 365 crore including NER components has been made.
(ii) ` 268.70 Crore (74% of total Budget) has been released under CSS-PT to States out of budget
of ` 365.00 Crore and proposal for release of 20% balance amount is being processed by this
office after receipt of proposal from different States. `345.00 Crores will be utilized through
release of funds to 50 Tiger Reserves in 18 tiger range states based on their Annual Plan of
Operation (APO), Village Relocation, Research work, use of Modern technology, Man-Animal
Conflict, etc.
19.7 As regards Project Elephant, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change submitted
that the Budget estimate for Project Elephant for 2016-17 was `25.00 crores which was reduced to
`20.00 crores at Revised Estimate stage. The reduction was made by the Finance Division based on
expenditure incurred by the State Governments of Elephant Range States. The main reasons for shortfall
are delay release in fund to implementation agencies by the State Governments. For the year 2017-18,
Budget Estimate is `27.50 Crores. Chief Wildlife Wardens have been requested to submit Annual Plans
of Operation by 28/02/2017, so that the expenditure under the scheme can be made by the State
Governments from beginning of the financial year itself. The Project Elephant Division is regularly
pursing submission of Annual Plan of Operation as well as expenditure progress with concerned State
Governments.
19.8 The Committee notes the reasons furnished by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and
Climate Change for reduction in allocation of Project Tiger and Project Elephant at RE stage in
2016-17. Getting funds at RE stage for projects of national importance and then surrendering the
funds on account of low-expenditure incurred by the concerned State Governments is really
disappointing. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate
Change must impress upon the concerned State Governments to proactively plan their Annual
Plan of Operations and release the funds to implementation agencies so that the funds could be
utilized timely, so that the budget allocations made are not reduced.
(c) Integrated Development of Wildlife Habitats

December 2008 during Eleventh Plan to provide for a broad spectrum of conservation interventions in

19.12 During the meeting, the Committee also expressed apprehension about the shifting of some extra
lions from Gujarat to Madhya Pradesh. In this context, the Committee was informed by the Ministry that
carnivore populations restricted to a single site is prone to various epidemic as well as natural calamities
or retaliatory killings, which may result into their extinction. Considering this fact, reintroduction of
Asiatic lion which is restricted only to Gir Landscape in Gujarat, an alternative site to ensure their long
term viability was proposed. After ecological assessment of some Protected Areas within the historical
range of Lions, the Wildlife Institute of India (WII) identified Kuno Palpur Sanctuary, Madhya Pradesh
as the most potential site for reintroduction. In this regard, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its
judgment dated 15th April, 2013 directed MoEF&CC to constitute an Expert Committee under the
Chairmanship of ADG (WL) to oversee the Lion reintroduction from Gir to Kuno Palpur Sanctuary as
per the IUCN Guidelines for translocation.

31
19.13 The Committee had visited Gir Forest in Gujarat on the 17th January 2017 to study the issues
relating to Gir Forest and held discussion with the NGOs/Civil Society Organisations, State Forest
Department, Government of Gujarat and Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change on
the issues relating to Gir Forest.
19.14 The Committee was informed by the representatives of the State Forest Department that the Gir
ecosystem can take legitimate pride in saving critically endangered Asiatic lion from the threshold of
extinction at the beginning of twentieth century by affording it a relatively safe habitat. With timely and
prompt conservation efforts made by the Gujarat Forest Department, the Asiatic lion population increased
and dispersed to other areas also and formed different distant populations in the landscape. The most
important aspect of Gir Protected Area is that it has become very stable ecosystem with tremendous
regenerating, self-supporting and self-sustaining capability due to its rich and diverse flora and fauna and
intensive protection and management by Gujarat Forest Department. Along with Lion, this region also
supports many other rare and threatened flora and fauna.
19.15 The Committee was also informed that at present, the Greater Gir area is home to about 523
Asiatic lions distributed across the landscape in more than 22,000 sq. km. area. The present distribution
range of Asiatic lions, also called as "Asiatic Lion Landscape" (ALL) falls in the seven districts of
Saurashtra region of Gujarat State. ALL is also known for high density of large carnivore population in
many Protected Areas such as Gir National Park, Gir Sanctuary, Girnar Sanctuary, Pania Sanctuary,
Mitiyala Sanctuary and many other Reserved and Protected Forests.
19.16 It was also informed to the Committee that in spite of successful conservation efforts over last
five decades, registering sustained increasing population trend, the Asiatic lion is still endangered. Total
current population of Asiatic lion is only about one fourth of the population of another large Indian Cat,
the Bengal tiger  (Panthera tigris tigris). Therefore, the long term conservation of Asiatic lion warrants
equal; if not more conservation attention to that of Tiger. On the other hand there are potential opportunities
to strengthen and consolidate the Asiatic lion conservation in terms of strengthening lion conservation
in the areas where lions have recently dispersed. There is requirement for strategic developments for
landscape and regional approach for conservation of large carnivores with improved techniques and
technologies of handling large mammals, to manage rescue requirements, to address man-wild animal
conflict issues etc. There is also a need to intervene for integrated conservation and development
programmes such as eco-development, eco-tourism etc. With increased political will and advancement
in scientific technologies for genetic conservation of Asiatic Lions, captive gene-pool and cryo-preservation
of genes have been initiated.
19.17 The Committee was also informed that after declaration of Gir Sanctuary in 1965, conservation
efforts were accelerated and systematic studies were undertaken to understand the ecosystem of the
area. Conservation of the Asiatic lion is one of the priorities of the State Government of Gujarat as well
as that of the Government of India. The efforts of the State/Central Governments have borne fruits as
can be seen from the gradual increase in population and geographical spread of the Asiatic Lion in
Saurashtra region of Gujarat.

32
19.18 Lion is known as the King of the Forest. Today the number of lions in the country has
decreased and the need of the hour is to come forward to protect them and increase their
number. The Committee commends the role of the State Government of Gujarat for having
taken timely and prompt conservation efforts whereby the population of Asiatic lion has increased.
However, the Committee is also of the view that the Asiatic lion is still endangered on account
of its low population. The Committee is of the view that already a mechanism is in place for
providing statutory support for protecting Tigers and Elephants. In view of the reducing number
of the Lions, the Committee recommends that Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate
Change must take necessary steps for providing statutory support for strengthening lion
conservation and, on the lines of Project Tiger and Project Elephant, come up with a 'Project
Lion' to protect Lions and their habitat.
20. ISSUES RELATING TO GIR FOREST
20.1 During the meeting of the Committee held on 17th January 2017, the following points were
brought out by the members of the Civil Society/NGOs:
(i) Despite a large numbers of carnivores in and around the Gir forest, there were not much
cases of animal-human conflict involving lion and man.
(ii) There is a railway line inside the Gir Forest area and railway authorities wanted to build a
retiring room in the name of building a station for passengers even though no tourists come
inside the national park by train.
(iii) No hotels should be allowed to be constructed near the boundary wall of the national park.
Further, mining and other industries should also not be allowed in the vicinity of the national
park.
(iv) Local people should not be harassed in their farming activities. Many local roads have been
closed by the forest authorities which causes problems to the local people in their free
movement.
(v) Many lions die due to electrocution as farmers have electric barbed (wire) fencing outside
their fields.
(vi) There are three temples inside the forest area where large number of pilgrims visit leaving
behind huge amount of garbage inlcuidng plastic bottles etc. scattered in the forest.
(vii) Many trees have been cut in the forest leaving no place for nesting of vultures.
(viii) An Expert Committee of the Central Government has cleared the proposal of making 'Girnar
Ropeway' for the visiting tourists. However the local people expressed concern that due to
this ropeway, vulture's nesting/breeding would get affected.
(ix) There was non-availability of water bodies inside the national park. It was suggested to build
artificial water bodies inside the park.

33
(x) Lion population was increasing outside Gir Forest also and they were living in non-protected
areas. Hence, the areas where these lions are living should be acquired by purchasing. It
was also suggested that hills/mountains near forest area should not be allowed to be
demolished in any manner.
20.2 The representatives of State Forest Department, Government of Gujarat also made a presentation
before the Committee which included the overall spectrum of Gir Protected Areas viz.: National Perspective
on Wildlife Management; Historical Perspective on Asiatic Lions; Extent of Area of Gir Forest under
Management; Habitat Improvement Interventions; Status of Flora & Fauna of Gir; Population Status of
Asiatic Lions; Population Status of Herbivores; Reclaimed of Lost Territory; Eco-development activities;
Wildlife Tourism Management; Man-Animal Conflict Resolution; Budgetary Provisions for Gir Management;
Gujarat State Lion Conservation Society Establishment; and Future Challenges in Wildlife Management.
20.3 The Committee desired to know the reasons for low number of forest employees. In response,
the Committee was informed that 1500 forest guards were being recruited and will join very shortly. As
regards the income accruing from the national park, the Committee was informed that more than 5 lakhs
tourists visit the national park every year and entire income accruing therefrom is used in the national
park itself and for the benefit of local people.
20.4 During the meeting, the Committee was also informed that Eco-Sensitive Zone around National
Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries, as per existing guidelines of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and
Climate Change, should be 10 km. However, there was a move it reduce it to 500 meters for Gir Forest.
The local representatives informed the Committee that proposal to this effort had been approved by State
Government and sent to the Central Ministry. When, the Committee enquired into the matter, the
representative of the State Government stated that it is upto the Central Government to allow reducing
the eco-sensitive zone. When the Chairperson enquired from the representative of the Union Government
as to whether they have any fixed norm about it, the Committee was informed that the Central Government
generally went by the proposals of the State Governments.
20.5 In view of the above, the Committee strongly recommends to the Ministry of Environment,
Forest and Climate Change not to reduce the guidelines of eco-sensitive zone from existing 10
kms to proposed 500 meters by the State Government, as it will surely destroy the Lion habitat.
The Committee recommends that there should be uniformity regarding the declaration of Eco-
Sensitive Zones around National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries.
20.6 The Committee also recommends that Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate
Change and Government of Gujarat should look into the issues brought out above which were
raised by the members of the Civil Society and local representatives during the meeting. Further,
the Committee observes that Gir National Park is very poorly connected by air. The Committee
recommends that Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change and Government
should take up the matter with the concerned Central and State Government agencies so that
air connectivity to Gir Forest can be improved. Further, the Committee is of the view that policy
of granting license to dhabas/hotels being run near the national park needs to be reviewed
keeping in view of the fact that lot of garbage is generated and thrown by these dhabas/hotels

34
etc. in the area. The Committee also recommends that illegal construction or encroachment in
and around the national park should be viewed seriously and stringent steps must be taken in
this direction.
20.7 The Committee also agrees with the apprehension expressed that making 'Girnar Ropeway'
for the visiting tourists is likely to affect the vulture nesting/breeding. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Central Government should review the matter and take a decision in the
matter only after it has examined the report of the expert Committee threadbare.
21. ENVIRONMENTAL ISSUES OF RANN OF KUTCH/BHUJ
21.1 The Committee visited Rann of Kutch/Bhuj in Gujarat in January, 2017 to study the environmental
issues of these areas. The Committee visited Rann of Kutch on 19th January, 2017 and held discussion
with the representatives of NGOs/Civil Society organizations and State Government of Gujarat and
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change on environmental issues of Rann of Kutch and Bhuj
areas.
21.2 The Committee was informed by the representatives of the State Government that Kutch district
in Gujarat state covering an area of 45,674 sq. km. is the largest district of India. The population of
Kutch is 2,092,371 (2011). The district consists of 10 Talukas, 939 villages and 6 Municipalities. Kutch
District is surrounded by the Gulf of Kutch and the Arabian Sea in south and west, while northern and
eastern parts are surrounded by the Great and Little Rann (seasonal wetlands) of Kutch. Bhuj is the
district headquarters of Kutch District. The land of Kutch which supports forest vegetation mostly
consists of undulated plains with scattered hillocks therein. Some patches are in plains, some with deeply
cut riverbeds and larger tracts are of pasturelands.
21.3 The Committee was further informed that the Rann is a salt impregnated and wilderness area and
is often referred as 'saline waste'. The Rann is only a few feet above the mean sea level and is spread
over 23309 sq. kms. Rann of Kutch is divided into two parts; one to the north known as the Greater
Rann of Kutch and the other towards the east is known as the 'Little Rann of Kutch'. The Greater Rann
of Kutch consists of a vast expanse of tidal mud flats with saline efflorescence. Strata of northern strip
of Kutch belongs to the Jurassic period with recent alluvium on the low land. In the southern portion
of the Greater Rann of Kutch, there is a large stretch of alluvium called the 'Banni' having area of about
2497 sq. kms. It was informed that this tract seems to have been once a part of the Rann but later on
was covered by fresh alluvial deposits brought down by rives. In the hilly areas, the soil is very shallow
often existing only in the crevices of rocky areas.
21.4 Kutch is rich in biodiversity and is represented by diverse flora and fauna. The varied geographical,
geological and climatic conditions has blessed Kutch district with diverse forest areas ranging from grass
lands, arid tropical forests to mangrove vegetations. The forests are mainly distributed between two
divisions, Kutch east and Kutch west division which are a part of the Kutch forest circle formed for
administrative reasons. The details are as under:

21.9 It was also brought out that in the forest areas of Kutch, invasive plant species (Prosopis juliflora)

protect traditional grazing system and natural resources. It was also brought out that in non-forest areas
of Kutch, there was a need to strengthen Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) under PBR and
the Biological Diversity Act, 2002. It was also informed that at present, the Act was not being given
sufficient importance.

36
21.10 The following points were also brought out with respect to the grassland, Thorn Forest and
Coastal belt areas:
(i) Indiscriminate industry, especially ports and mining industry are compromising fisheries and
grasslands/thorn forests and therefore animal husbandry.
(ii) There needs to be planning (as landscape level) to designate areas where industries and
mining are allowed. This will also protect wildlife corridors and other biodiversity sites.
(iii) Seasonal resource/grazing patterns mapping of pastoralist communities to protect their
traditional livelihood and mainstreaming local people towards the conservation of ecosystems
and their threatened biodiversity.
(iv) Identified Ecologically Sensitive Areas (ESA) by GEC, IUCN, Researchers etc. should be
mapped with immediate action.
(v) In GIB (Great Indian Bustard) areas, wind mills and illegal encroachment should be mapped
for carrying capacity and proposed ESA by FD should be sanctioned to protect GIB and
other BD species in Abdasa area.
(vi) All the plantation activities should be monitored under CAMPA scheme i.e. Mangrove etc.
21.11 The Committee feels that the local people of Kutch deserve appreciation for their contribution
in developing and preserving whole landscape of the Rann of Kutch and congratulates them for
their dedication and commitment for preserving the landscape of Rann of Kutch.
21.12 The Committee feels that all the issues brought out in the preceding paragraphs deserve
attention and recommends that Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change and
Government of Gujarat to consider these issues and take necessary action. The Committee also
notes that a large number of tourists come to visit the Rann of Kutch and leave behind a lot
of garbage including plastic wrappers and bottles that lie scattered in that area. The Committee
is of the view that there is a need to ban the use of plastic wrappers. The Committee recommends
that heavy penalties should be imposed on violators and those found littering garbage. The
tourists visiting the place should also be sensitized about the need for maintain cleanliness in
the area. The Committee also feels that there is scarcity of water in the area. Although local
people of the area are doing their bit for water conservation and have even created pond having
recharging capacity using local traditional methods, the Committee recommends that the State
Government authorities must take necessary action for water harvesting so that the issue of
water scarcity in the area is resolved.
21.13 The Committee also recommends that the State Government of Gujarat must look into the
matter relating to transfer of the land adjoining the sanctuary to Forest Department of the State
Government in order to protect and preserve the endangered species of birds, especially Great
Indian Bustard and other animals. The State Government should also look into the matter
regarding wasteland management in the area, as requested by some local people there. Further,
the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should also undertake study on
bio-diversity of the entire Bhuj region and take necessary actions to preserve them.

22. PRIVATE LAND PARTICIPATION IN PRESERV ATION AND CONSERV ATION OF FORESTS
22.1 During the meeting of the Committee held on the 14th February 2017, the Committee desired to
know as to whether forests can be raised on private lands. The Committee had also received request
to this effect from some persons. Responding to the query of the Committee, the representative of the
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change responded as under:
"Madam, there was also a question on whether forests can be raised on private lands. Y es, they
can be raised on private lands. The issue of permission for tree-felling depends on the State as
well as on the species. Different States have different regulations. But the local regulations would
apply and we welcome if anyone wants to raise tree plantations on their land. It is going to add
to the tree cover of the country."
22.2 Some of the suggestions received by the Committee that should form the fundamental framework
in this context are as under:
• This should apply to only private lands and restriction of 'Rural land Ceiling' should not apply.
• Participation should be a voluntary process, which cannot be reversed for perpetuity.
• The owner's easement on the entire land should remain intact. This includes sale or transfer
without any change in the nature of the land i.e. permanent preservation of the forest.
• Restriction on area that can be developed (Not exceeding 5% for instance).
• Encouragement of Eco-friendly agriculture, nature/wildlife tourism, flora and fauna reintroduction
programs and research.
• Monetary compensation only in form of Income Tax Breaks over a long period of time, say
20 to 30 years (To bring in sincere participation and not make it another tax break tool).
• 'Cooperation framework' to work with the forest departments.
22.3 The Committee feels that as the forest cover of the country has been drastically and
constantly depleting, there is a need to involve private sector in increasing the forest cover of
the country by encouraging private land participation in preservation and conservation of forests.
There are a lot of people in the country who are having large landholdings and that they would
be happy to contribute to increasing the forest cover of the country. This would also give a boost
to the shrinking forest cover of the country. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of
Environment, Forest and Climate Change should consider the suggestions received by the
Committee as mentioned above. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should
consider giving tax exemptions and compensations to those who proposed to raise forests on the
big areas of land available with them. They should be incentivized only when the land available
with them grows as forest, so that the green area cover of the country grows. This will not only
increase India's forest cover, meet some of the green India mission requirements but also bring
in much needed private participation in conservation and preservation of forests.

ZOOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
The Committee recommends that Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
should look into all the above issues that emerged during the meeting with the representatives
of ZSI and take necessary action thereon, as the Committee feels that all these issues merit full
consideration. (Para 10.5)
The Committee is of the view that certain specimens conserved in ZSI are irreplaceable and
some of them have even become extinct in our country. The specimens are our national assets
and they should be conserved befittingly. It is sad and alarming to note that due to resource
constraints, the concerned authorities are unable to preserve the specimen with modern
technologies. The Committee recommends that the entire building of ZSI should be upgraded and
modernised in a time bound manner, on a top priority basis. The rooms/boxes where the specimens
are kept should be temperature controlled. The modernization of the building would also enable
the specimens to be displayed in a way so that visitors could have a good look at them. ZSI is
one the country's most valuable resource centers and, therefore, the building and the conservation
areas should be modernised in a manner reflecting their importance and their place in Indian
history. The Committee also recommends that adequate budgetary allocation should be made for
the renovation and modernisation of the building and the specimen conserving/preserving areas.
(Para 10.7)
BOTANICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
The Committee is in agreement with the view that the knowledge of taxonomy was
deteriorating fast in the country. The Committee observes that the existing staff in BSI is only
55% of the sanctioned strength, which includes huge vacancies in almost all the categories of
posts. The Committee is at a loss to understand as to how, with a highly depleted manpower
strength, the organisation would be able to perform its constitutional obligations. The Committee
also notes that the BSI has been able to expend only nearly 55% of the budgetary allocation upto
January, 2017. The Committee recommends that Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate
Change should take all necessary action, on priority basis, to ensure that the huge number of
vacancies in different categories of posts, are filled up at the earliest. The Committee also
recommends that the BSI should be strengthened both by infrastructure as well as by trained
manpower and the skills of rapidly declining number of taxonomists should be augmented to
meet the enormous task of documenting the plant and animal resources of the country. Adequate
funds should also be made available to the BSI for the purpose. (Para 11.5)
The Committee was also informed that the persons holding senior positions in BSI would
be retiring shortly and the new recruitment would be done at a junior level only. This would
result in a huge gap in the talent available in the Institution. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should devise measures
to improve the capacity building in the Institution by temporarily utilising the talent presently
available till such time the gap in talent requirement is reduced. (Para 11.6)

CHIRU GOAT (TIBETAN ANTELOPE)
The Committee feels that Jammu and Kashmir has been the conflict region for long and
many women there are unable to leave their homes and go out for livelihood. The shawl walas
who live there have been accused of killing the chiru goat in order to procure the wool for
making a shahtoosh shawl. However, the shawl makers say that they do not kill the goats
because if they kill a goat for every shawl, where will the shawls be produced from. The
Committee understands that China and Mongolia are breeding the chiru goats and Mongolia is
known for its finest wool. The Committee feels that livelihood opportunities are very low for the
people of Jammu and Kashmir because of the extreme climatic conditions there and shawl
making contributes a lot towards sustainable livelihoods of these people. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should conserve and
breed the chiru goat and vast tract of land should be utilized for conserving the chiru goats.
These goats can then be given to the shawl makers for collecting hair. This would not only
increase the number of these goats but would also add to the sustainable livelihood opportunities
of the people of Jammu and Kashmir , who are a lot dependant on the handicraft of embroidered
shawls. (Para 15.2)

LEAPFROGGING FROM BS-IV TO BS-VI STANDARDS OF EMISSION FOR FUEL VEHICLES

Air pollution from motor vehicles is not only emitted directly into the atmosphere but also from
chemical reactions between pollutants after they have been released into the air. The Committee
notes the initiatives taken by the Ministry of Environment, Forests & Climate Change on
leapfrogging from BS-IV to Bharat Stage-VI norms. The Committee recommends that there
should be no let up in the efforts of the Ministry of Environment, Forests & Climate Change

Lion is known as the King of the Forest. Today the number of lions in the country has
decreased and the need of the hour is to come forward to protect them and increase their
number. The Committee commends the role of the State Government of Gujarat for having
taken timely and prompt conservation efforts whereby the population of Asiatic lion has increased.

of its low population. The Committee is of the view that already a mechanism is in place for
providing statutory support for protecting Tigers and Elephants. In view of the reducing number

Change must take necessary steps for providing statutory support for strengthening lion
conservation and, on the lines of Project Tiger and Project Elephant, come up with a 'Project
Lion' to protect Lions and their habitat. (Para 19.18)
